DISENTHRONED. She held her court in our parlour, Oar tiny cousin May, And the wee ones gathered round her In frolic and noisy play. We praised her Bunny tresses • And her brown eyes bright with glee. "In all the town," we chorused, "There is no such baby as she 1" Alas, we had quite forgotten Our winsome, blue-eyed Roy, Till we heard a great sob breaking From the lips of our baby boy; And with big tears coursing downwards He whispered falteringly, "Dere's a 'ittle boy at our house As 'tannin' as he can be:" —Geed Cheer (American).
THE QUESTIONER. I ask not for his lineage?
I ask not for his name? If manliness be in his heart, He noble birth may claim. I care not though of world's wealth,
But slender be his part, If yes, you answer, when I ask, HAW he a true man's heart?
I ask not from what land he came.?
. _ Or where his youth was nursed? If pure the stream, what matters it, The spot from whence it burst?

7he palace or the hovel, Where first his life begul, I ask not of, but, tell me this, Is he an honest man? Nay, blush not thou, what matters it Where first he drew his breath? A manger was the cradle bed Of Him of Nazareth.
Be nought, be any, everything, I care not what you be, If yes, you answer, when I ask Is he pure, true, and free? ROBERT WICIIOLL.

BROUGHAM AND LEGAL VEELBOSITY.—A certain barrister named Jones, who practised in Broughetn's time, contracted hta habit of commencing the examination of a witness with these words—" Now, sir, I am going to put a question to you, and I don't care which way you answer it.', Brougham had beg,..,n, like many others, to grow tired of this eternal for:rule. One morning he met his brother lawyer near the Temple, and addressed him thus—" Now, Jones, I am ping to pot a question to you, and I don't care which way you answer it--How do you do ?" BATiNG GRAPES IN BuSele.—Once an accomplished young Aineadetn woman had the honour to dine with the Czar, of Russia. During the entertainment a plate of grapes was paned. The young lady saw the golden knife on the basket, but as the fruit came to her first, she had no way of learning its use; so she did just as she would have done in • America—reached out her dainty fingers and lifted from the dish a whole stem of grapes. What was her consternation to see the next person, as well as all the other guests, take the golden knife and sever a single grape each, and transfer it to their plates. THE SPECTRUM OF THE LARGE COMET.—SediIIM and carbon have been discovered by means of the spectroscope to be present in the large comet. The carbon rays resemble those given out by a hydro-carbon gas when excited by the electric discharge, and the theory that the cometary tail is a vast electric arc light gains in favour. BLEACHING DIAMONDS.—The yellow tine of Cape dia- monds reduces their price very considerably, and an attempt has been made recently to make them look white. This is dons by immersing the stone in any solution of a blue tint which is the complementary colour of its natural yellow tinge. The result is that a thin laver of blue adheres to the stone and quenches the yellow light, making the gem look as if it were of the first water. To bring back the native colour, however, it is only necessary to wash the stone. The apparent bleaching is only " skin•deep." IRIDIUM•TIPPED SAW-TF,ETlL—Advantage has been taken of recent discoveries and improvements in the working of Iridium—a refractory and extremely hard metal—to intro- duce it in the manufacture of cutting tools. A circular saw, twelve inches in diameter, has been made, the teeth of which were tipped with iridium. As the saw in question has been devised specially for the purpose of sawing the hardest woods, it will be seen that the employment of iridium in this capacity will probably be attended with the beet results, and lead to a more extended application of the metal in this direction. There is but one serious drawback Ito the use of iridium, however, and that is that it happens ' to be one of the rare metals. MAGNIFICENT DISPLAY OF AURORA. BOREALIS.—One Of the most beautiful displays of aurora that has ever been witnessed at Lerwick took place on Sunday night. The lights first commenced-to uppeer low down in the northern heavens, and gradually extended to the east and west, rising higher no in the sky, and forming many different shapes. I The first distinct form they assumed was that of a beautiful belt, of a light bluish colour, which spanned the whole Inorthern sky from east to west, with streamers darting from it, right down to the horizon. In the next moment the form was changed. The lights then assumed a magnificent appearance. The streamers darted up towards the zanitb, and the bluieb belt, extending upwards, took the form of an immense curtain, spreading over the whole northern sky. Massive fold, exactly resembling those of a heavy hanging curtain, were distinctly formed, and momentarily the lower edges of the folds assumed ever-changing colours of the most beautiful hues, flashing along with lightning rapidity from west to east. This magnificent spectacle disappeared In a few moments, but the forms it took as it disappeared were it anything, even more beautiful. The curtain was endAely parted in the centre, and then rolled away to the east and west, the e.iges of both sides turning round and round like a scroll, and still baeutifully tinted. Faint bluish lights anceeetied, which again assumed many pretty shapes. The display commenced about eight o'clock, and was most brilliant during the succeeding 30 minutes, but for several boars afterwards the lights were a conspicuous object in the heavens. Nothing so brilliant as this display was witnessed when the aurora was observed in December last, although the lines then were of longer duration and spread over a great expanse of sky. LOCOMOTIVE SPEED INDICATOR.—A. new indicator for recording the exact speed of the train during the whole run, and all the stoppages and startiogs wish the exact time of each, has been invented by M. Pouget, French honorary Inspector-general of telegraphs. It is manufactured by M. Paul Gamier, and was recently described by M. Briill before the Soeiet6 des Ingeoieurs Civils. It consists of two distinct portions, the first consisting of a special clock, the dial of which indicates the time, and which causes to revolve, on a horizontal axis, the drum to which a sheet of white paper Is attached. The drum is also made to travel latterly by means of a fixed screwi baying the same axis as the arbor of the clock so that each point of the sheet of paper des- cribee a helix. The second portion of the apparatus com- prises the mean, whereby it derives its motion from the locomotive, and a combination of hammers and styles for affording the various indications. Motion is obtained Irons one of the locomotive tires, preferably one to which no brake is applied, by means of a small roller slightly rounded, and kept pressing against it by means of small springs. The motion is transmitted by suitable mechanism to a racket wheel, which makes one revolution for every kilometre traversed, and is delivered into forty equal parts by pro- jecting points, which mark every 25 metres run through. At the end of each kilometre a spring 'hammer strikes the head of a style. Y:ti These marks -of distance traversed are underlined when the locomotive runs backwards. The paper is divided into fifteen columns, 20 millimetres wide, and into bands 7 millimetres high, each band representing a quarter of annour. The bands hive an obliquity of 7 metres in their lengthAso that, when the sheet is rolled on the dram, and the ends are united, a continuous helix is formedirbe hours are not marked on the paper beforehand, because, as the whole sheet only represents a space of five or six hours, it is more convenient, so as the better to utilise the paper and not leaves spaces, to note, at the moment of placing the sheet on the drum, the hour corre- sponding to the first bands. When the station-master gives the denial for starting, he presses a spring, which makes a mark on the paper. If the driver starts at once, the distance marks laTin at once; but, if he be not ready, the number of minutes lost are shown by the sheet. The appliance is solidly constructed, so as not to be liable to damage by the shakes due to irregularities of the road, and it is enclosed in a plate-iron box to prevent:any tampering. A VISIT TO EASTER ISLAND.—Commander B)LiVelie F. Clark, in her Majesty's ship Sappho, visited Easter leland, that remote outlying', member of the Polynesian island groups, so remarkable for its stone sculptures and remains of native architecture' in June last. The Sappho sighted the island on the 17th day from Coquimbo, and anchored on the evening of the same day in Cook Bay. On passing the village of Maltveri the English flag was seen hoisted on a long flazstaff, and shortly after landing the vessel was boarded by Mr. Alexander Salmon, the agent of the" /Alison Brander," of Tahiti, who now owns the greater part of the Island. From him, daring the two days' stay of the vessel, Commander Clark obtained the information he had to give regarding the island. The Maison Brander four years ago purchased the property of the missionaries on the island, who then left for the Gambier Archipelago, taking about 300 of the netives with them. A large grazing farm was established, and there are now about 10,000 sheep and 400 heed of cattle on the islaud ; the flocks increase very raehily, as there aro two, and sometimes three, lambing sea- ;sns in the ytar. With the present number of sheep Mr. Salmon gets about 15 tons of wool per annum. There are enormous numbers of poultry in the island in a semi-wild state, but all owned by the natives; in fact, a fleet could easily be supplied with fresh provisions, except vegetables; but 29 yams, sweet potatoes, bananas, and plantains grow readily, they also could be supplied in time. Water is the only scarce article. The natives :lOW remaining are only 150 in number, bat they art Oft the decrease. About 500 were shipped to Tahiti some eight years ago to work on the plantations of the Matson Brander, besides the three hun- dred removed by the missionaries. ,Among those remain- ing there are no traces of the missionaries' work ; the have no religion at all, are expert thieves, and very re- vengeful; they never:forget or forgive, although in general good tempered. They are divided into several small clans, among which strength or personal courage is the only claim to superiority, and their chief quarrels arise over the efforts of each clan to secure the first eggs of the " wide-awake " every year from Needle Rock, to which they attach a super- stitions value. As there is a heavy surf at the bottom of the cliffs opposite the rock, several lives are lost nearly every year while they are seeking for the eggs. eThe result of Mr. Salmon's repeated talks with the natives,' on the sub- ject of their first arrival in the island is to find that they all say they originally landed on the north side of Anakena, and (aura from the east in two canoes, provisioned with yams, taro, and sweet potatoes, the king (by name Hoto- metva, or the "Prolific Father ") in one canoe, and the queen in the other. On making the land they separated, passing round in opposite directions and meeting again at Anakena, where they landed and settled 'on Mount Topaze, of which the native name is Hoto-iti. They there built the stone houses the remains of which atill:exist, and made the statues with which the hill is covered; but the first statue was not made till some fifty years after they landed. The natives say the original name of the island was not Rapanui but Te-pito-fenva—i.e , the land in the middle of the sea. Commander Clark was much struck with the evident fer- tility of the soil. If it were only cultivated he believed it would produce magnificent crops, and it seemed to him especially adapted for the cultivation of vines. The extinct volcano of Te Ran:a Kao, on the south-west corner of the island, is well worthy of a visit. The bottom of the crater is not'level, as described by a former visitor; on the con- trary, there is no bottom at 50 fathoms in the centre, but there is a carpet of decayed vegetation spread over the water on which One can cross from side to side.

The death is announced of Mr. Thomas Scott, late farmet at Gateside, on the Moncreiffe estate, Perthshire. He has been altogether about 85 years on the Moncreiffe property, having served under four lairds.

A ss bepherd named Chisholm ha been arrested by the Perthshire police on a charge of steallng a lot of 82 black- Linea sheep from a farm at Lochearnslde, several weeks ago. A daring robbery of sheep is reported from the neighbour- hood of Hawarden. Two of a flock belonging to one of Mr. Gladstone's tenants were killed in the field, and the carcases carried away. The skins were left.

The Netvc- astle Chronicle states that two sheep, belonging to Mr. C. Hetherington, of Myrtle Bank, West Allendale, were lost in the late storm, and no hope was entertained of recovering them alive, but, strange to say, they were found the other day by the sheep dog in an old quarry. They had been under the snow 18 days, and endeavoured to supply themselves with food by eating the wool off one another. Mr. Wood, of Rsasay, has promised to supply his tenants next spring with change of potato seed, free of charge, and they can therefore consume all the potato crop of this year for food. Besides this, Mr. Wood has given a reduction of rent to the extent of one-third, and made payments to seve- ral tenants for .damage done to their crops by gams. The agricultural college at Montpellier, France, has so far outgr .wn its limits that the Ministry of Agriculture are about to expend £lO.OOO on the purchase of the adjoining estate of Gaillar le, and a further sum of £B,OOO in the con- eiruction and enlargement of the college premises. In the department of the E we-et-Loire over 79,000 sheep were operated upon in 1892, end on these the mortality was reduced from 9 per cent. to 0 65 Der cent. Several bulls realised good prices, Mr. G. Elliott, of Queensland, being an . extensive purchaser at prices ranging from 400 gs. down to 200 gs. The bull Eighth Duke of Tregunter, four years old, was started at 1,000g5., and advanced to 4,000g5., at which price he was purchased by Mr. Gardiner. This sum is said to be the highest ever realised in the Colonies for any bovine animal. REFRIGERATED MILE IN AUSTRdLIA.—It appears that In Sydney, New South Wales, something practical is being done in the way of bringing the milk to the city from the country districts. The Fresh Food and Ice Company re- ceives and distributndaily about 5,000 quarts of milk, be- sides quantities of cream and butter, raised or made at its depot on the south coast. These 5,000 quarts are received from farmers in the south coast dairy district, which stretches nearly from Sydney to the Victorian border, and of which Klima is the centre ; some of it comes by rail and some by steamer. The company finds its own trucks, specially fitted for the trade. On the arrival of the milk in Sydney it is weighed, teated by various kinds of lactometere, ii! led by machinery into vats in a cold room, and there agitated, to prevent the cream rising, until it is wanted. So low is the temperature that it can be kept for a month. It is led by :machinery to the delivery-room, and is there weighed out. THE VALUATION OF WAXWING CROPS or TURNIPS.— There is frequent difficulty in valuing the turnip crop of an outgoing tenant in fixing upon the basis of valuation. An illustration in point is reported from Kirkcudbright. An outgoing tenant in that county was by his lease bound to give the incoming tenant the option of taking the waygoing crop of turnips at "valuation by two arbiters mutually chosen," Sec., all in the usual form. Of this option the in- coming tenant availed himself. But difficulties arose as to whether the arbiters were to fix the price at such a figure as the turnips would bring to be eaten on the land by sheep, as had been the custom during the currency of the tack, or whether the price should be such as the crop would bring if sold in Liverpool (less carriage, of course). It seems there are facilities for shipment near the farm. The arbiters, though the submission to them appears to have been plenary, declined to decide the point in dispute, and consequently agreed to make two valuations. If the contention of the outgoing tenant is given effect to, the price to be paid for the turnips will be about £2OO beyond their value for the purpose of being eaten on the ground by sheep. EXPERIMENTAL FARMING.—A very interesting experi- ment has been carried out by Mr. W. H. Hargood, a farmer on the Mendip Hills. That gentleman, with a view of ascer- taining what quantity, if any, of nutritious matter such plants as beans draw or imbibe from the air around us' set on the 30th of May, eight horse beans in a wooden box which was filled with silver sand washed thoroughly clean, placing the box some distance above the ground to prevent anything being absorbed therefrom. The beans came up in due aeasor, and progressed well in growth and blossomed, the plants producing altogether 24 pods, in which were a total of 47 beans. During the entire existence of these plants nothing whatever was supplied to them but pure water. When the stalks and leaves were black and dead and the pods ripe, the plants were drawn from the sand. Roots, haulms, pods, and leaves were all further dried in an open place under cover from wet fer three weeks, the whole mass, including the beans in the pods, then weighing, after being thus thoroughly dried, 1,010 grains, the 47 beans by them- selves weighing 329 grains. The eight beans that were set weighed 56 grains. Others have tried similar experiments, and it has been asked by them, and with reason, "From what source has this increase in weight been derived ?" The plants could not have fed on the sand in which they grow, and the water which they consumed, being to all in tents and purposes pure, could contribute nothing to their sustenance, and yet the 56 grains of bean seed enlarged to 1,040 grains of organic substance, or nearly 20 times its original weight in 13 Weeks. The total of 47 beans found in the pods weighed, as before stated, 329 grains, or close upon six times the weight of the seed planted. At the same time as the above beans were planted the writer, set nine other horsebeans in another wooden box, fixing it a foot and a half from the ground as in the previous case, and filling it also with clean-washed silver sand. These plants were watered with a weak solution of manure, composed of superphos- phate of lime, mariate of potash, and sulphate of lime. They came up and grew well and bloomed, and when they were ripe the roots were drawn and all thoroughly dried, and treated exactly as to the other test, the whole then weighing 2,850 grains, and notwithstanding, as is generally known, beans are themselves rich in nitrogen. TENANT FARMERS' ANSWERS TO "Alm wet TO LOSE OUR FUTURE HARVESTS r—Will you kindly publish the results obtained by tenant-farmers with Gibbs' hay dryer ? At Reading, The Times said: "If Mr. Gibbs' or any other system can deal with such stuff as this, there ought never to be another load of hay spoilt, let the weather be what it may." The "stuff" that was pieced through my harvest- saver was finished off finally and completely in six hours, requiring nothing more to be done to it. This explains and confirms the voluntary statements made by Mr. Fuller, of Neaten Park, and Mr. Morris, of Wood Eaton Manor, ;hat even the £3io and £3BO harvest-savers repay their cost in two to three seasons. Surely a machine that will do this must be a good investment on every large farm. With the second size (£210) a tenant-farmer saved more than its total cost in one season on a single crop off 50 acres. A third size (£l2O portable, £lOO stationary) Is now constructed, and where stack-ccoling is used this machine is calculated to wither or drive out water-wet from the crop at the rate of Bto 10 acres a day. All these machines are available for corn crops as well as hay, and will restore mouldy stacks to fair value; this has been done at Reading with the mouldy stacks spoilt by the stack-cooling fans. By a simple addi- tion they can be converted into portable kilns. Mr. Roddick, of Qaintain Hill, Waltham Abbey, says :—" Nineteen loads of damaged hay, which would otherwise have been useless, were rendered fit for stacking at the rate of two loads and a half per hour. I realised £6O to £7O by the day-and-a-half's use of the hay-dryer." Mr. Amersfoordt, of ilaarlem, in- vited a gathering of 4,000 of the chief people in Holland to see his in action, and afterwards wrote :—" Grass that had been cut a couple of days was made into hay in five minutes, and was then immediately stacked with perfect safety. The horses eat it eagerly. I consider the trial perfectly success- ful." Later report from Mr. Fuller, Aug. 28, 1881 I am now feeding twenty steers On the machine-made hay; my herdsman tells me they have improved most rapidly, and eat the whole of it up clean." First report from Neston Park :—" Forty-three acres cut, 30 tons made in twenty- . .

three hours; cost 9s. ad. per acre, or 13s. 61. per ton, in- cluding cutting, making, and stacking, wet hay dried with- out shelter; rain felling frequently." Second report:— " Thirty-three acres cleared in twenty hours at ;m"ner less cost than above; hay stack.d in fine condition, the whole Working therougbly eatisfectory ; am convinced it will pay to use the process in all seasons." First report from Lord Ashburton, Grange Farm, Alresford :—" Twenty waggon loads dried and stacked on Friday, twenty-four on Saturday, and fifteen in six hours on Monday." Second report "Cleared 19 acres water-meadow grass ; average cost, 103 61 per acre; cut July 16, stacked on the 24th. Farmer in adjoining meadow cut his on July 15, could not finish stacking till August 11, and his hay is all spoilt." First re- port from Wood Eaton Manor :—" Seventy loads in three and a quartar days; clearing fields at rate of 12 acres a day." Second report —" Thirty-five ton of clover saved in five days, that would otherwise have been spoilt." Mr. S. Leather, of Delamere Lodge, near Nertlovich, borrowed Mr. Ainsworth's hay-dryer, and with it dried 341 loads, chiefly wet clover, in ninety-four hours. He says :—" This machine did splendid work, and entirely to my satisfaction; all kinds, of stock ate the hay ravenously, and in preference to that dried in the usual way."—To these let me add that Mr. Beale, of Chiddingstone, another_tenaut-farmer, found it _ _

thoroughly worth while to pay £2O for the loan of a small harvest-saver for his second crop alone, and saved about 170 acres with it ; also Mr. Taylor, of Compton Abdale, gladly borrowed Lord Ashburtoh's from Belding for a guinea and a half a day, and saved about 120 loads of barley that had lain out six or seven weeks. Also that Mr. Botling, a tenant-farmer of the Duke of Northumberland, saved the whole cost of a £2lO machine in a single season. I am quite aware that these larger machines are above the means of average tenant-farmers, and have always told them so, ad- vising them, at the same time, to get their landlords to adopt them so as first to save their own harvests, and after- wards those of their tenants.—W. A. Gis7,s.

CATS—BRONCHITIL.—From their fondness for wandering cats are very subject to bronchial affections, and the habit which some persons have of turking the cat out of doors at night—we hope none of our readers are so cruel and BO thoughtless—is a very prolific cause of them. Bronchitis proper begins with the symptons of a common cold, such as a staring coat, shivering and slight cough. Then the cat becomes very ill consequent of the acute stage of the com- plaint, which continues for a day or two, and if not checked soon passes into the chronic form. This is characterised by apparent difficulty of breathing, the cat is constantly cough- ing, with the tongue hanging over the lower lip, and there is an anxious expression about the face, the eyes watering and have a tendency to matter. If allowed to go on, she rapidly gets thinner, and hangs disconsolately about, at one time refusing all food, but at another eating enormously, but with a very depraved appetite. The best method of Cure is to confine the animal to one room. If nothing else can be done, put her in sa large roomy hamper, but be sure the door is securely fastened before she is allowed out of the same. Keep warm and feed on beef-tea and bread, or mile and arrowroot, with beef-tea. As medicine, the beat cure we know of is homeopathic tinctere of Waite, two or three drops of which should be put in the food, as this is the hest I way to give them it. When the bronchitis itself has been i cured, get up the strength by giving a teaspoonful of cod 1 liver oil for a fortnight. Or whit may be more easily ad- ministered, a cod liver oil capsule each time instead. Good food will, of course, oe necessary also. SNAKES As Parse—The probability is that many readers will be considerably astonished to see the heading above this note, as they have no idea that anyone will keep as pets what they will probably characterise as "nasty, shiny, dan- gerous things," but, strange though it may appear, it is none the less a fact that there are many people who do keep them, and declare themselves very fond of them. The writer could name many persons of note who have them, and his own introduction to the hobby was through an eminent scientist who has kept them for years. The gentleman states that they are about the best pets that he has ever kept, giving the least trouble, need very little care, and are quite capable of trebling and soon learn to know anyone who is kind to them. They can be kept in a drawer locked up, and will be quite comfortable if enveloped in a blanket or rug. If a sudden call from home causes them to be for- gotten they can be left without feed for a month or t and will suffer no ill consequences therefrom, so that there is no fear of servants neglecting their duties, as is the case with so many other pets. In playing with them—for only a few of the species are poisonous, but these have snfficed to give the whole race a bad name—there is no danger what. ever, so long as fear is not shown. If they seize the hand, as they often do in fun, they do not actually bite but simply hold it firmly. Not resisted they soon lose their hold, but if the hand is suddenly snatched away, they will probably grip tighter and a wound or a scratch be the result. Of course, only the smaller varieties or young snakes Can be se kept, as larger ones would from their strength be really dangerous inmates of any hoese. More upon this question we shall say as opportunity offers. RARBITS.—FOOD AND FEEDING.—A 3 promised in one of our earlier notes, we now return to the question of food for rabbits. The first thing is to impress upon every one who keeps them the great necessity of giving dry food. About seven in the morning they should have wheat, buckwheat, or barley, with a small piece of turnip or carrot, or, when obtainable, a small handful of green stuff. The second feed should consist of bay and green food, and be given about mid-day. The third and last, say about six o'clock in the evening, should consist of oats, with a handful of cut hay. Green food should not be given wet, but is best cut and allowed to wilt before using. Maize is a fairly:good morning feed, especially in cold weather, when main meal, mixed with hot skim milk, will make a most excellent food. It should, however, be covered close for half an hour until It is steamed through, so that the mess is not too soft. Half soaked peas are good, and cabbage is not bad, but all, whe- ther greens, beet, or carrot tops, should be given in small quantities, as too mach green or wet vegetable food is Sure to produce sickness, pot belly and dropey being caused this • way. A good cure for redwater is in dandelion tops or roasted potatoes. Dried tea leaves, fennel, parsley, chicory, • or aniseed are All useful as condiments when the appetite wants a little stimulating ; one vessel should not be used for both wet and dry food, and it is most important that the , troughs should be thoroughly cleansed out before any fresh food is put in, as rabbits have a very strong aversion to food upon which they have breathed before. In all cases should the food be given regularly, and great cleanliness observed ' in all dishes and troughs as well as in the hutchee them- ' selves. The disgesting state of some rabbitries not only ' makes the inmates uncomfortable, but at the same time is a most prolific cause of disease. Vermin, too, are harboured . and encouraged in dirty hutches, and, in fact, almost every trouble which the rabbit keeper can have may be brought on by neglect of the ordinary rules of cleanliness. Sick rabbits should never be kept with healthy ones, not only be- cause they require special food, but also because the food may be the means of communicating the disease from one to another.

DOGS —TRAINING FOR THP; GUY.—Contintling the re- marks from last week on this question, which we condense from a work entitled" !he Complete Sportsman," published in 1817, by T. H. Needham, we find next: When your dog stands steady at his point, walk deliberately up to him, on no account appearing in haste or running, for if you run he will be apt to do the same. If the birds run, let him follow them as cautiously as possible, and if he is impatient caution him by such words as "Be careful," or "Take head." If this is not enough he must be correeted severely. In a little time the dog should become perfectly steady id the point, but apt to run when the birds spring. For this he must be , brought hack to the place whence he ran, made to crouch, reprimanded with tha word "Down," and with the whip also if the word is not enffictently effective. In shooting, even if a bird is killed within a few feet of his nose, he ought not to be suffered to move until you have re-loaded. Therefore, In training with the loviirg piecr, ftonmel him to crouch or .the lie down on the spot for a considerable time art e: birds have taken wing, when a wave of the hand or a cry will it I sufficient to set him in motion. It is often difficult to pre- vent a dog from chasing a hare if one starts, but after ho has bosoms accustomed to see them, he will learn to set them and not ran after them. It almost uniformly happens, how- ever well a dog may be trained, that, when you come to fire over him at game, he will break away on the report of the fowling piece. He muet be brought back, spoken to angrily, using the words "Do xr, till charged." Then let the dog observe you re-load, and if you have killed a bird, let him hunt carefully up to it, with the word "Seek." Unlese pre• vented he might pull the bird to pieces, but must be checked by " Ware, deal." For correction, ha must be treated In the way most suitable to his temper and disposition, some dogs requiting severe flagellation and others much less. Should the bird have been winged merely, so much the better for a young dog—let him foot up to it. It sometimes hip. pens:however, that a young dog is not equal to this task, upon perceiving which', you must call in the assistance of an old dog, or you will lose the bird. Dogs can be trained before going into the field by tiring a pistol over their heads, and in many cases this may be a decided advantage. div.head: "OUR OLD NOBILITY.
div.p: "OUR OLD NOBILITY.
[Published by Mr. E. J. Kibbleiohite, 31, Tavistock-street London, W.C., and reprinted by permission] THE BRUGES.

The Bruees are a Norman family:, who came over with the Conqueror, and obtained large grants of land in the North of England. Ii the reign of Henry I. one of them, having ingratiated himself with the King of Scotland, obtained from that Monarch large grants of land in Annandale and, not long after, the Braces became allied by marriage with the Scottish Royal House. For some time the Braces were half English, half Scotch. Robert Bruces's father had a house near London, at Tottenham, Middlesex, the name of which is still preserved in Bruce Castle School, which was opened as a branch of the Birmingham establishment kept by the Messrs. Hill more than a generation ago. The English estates of the Bruces were confiscated in the time of the Plantagenets ; and England knew them not again as landowners till the beginning of the seventeenth century. From one of the younger branches of the Bruce family was descended Sir Edward Bruce? of Kinloss, who was em- ployed by King James in several embassies to the Court of Elizabeth, and who became the intermediary of that Monarch's confidential correspondence with the younger Cecil before his accession to the English Crown. Like the rest of the needy Scottish courtiers, Bruce accompanied his master to England; and, in the very first year of James's reign, obtained for life the great place of Master of the Rolls. The following year he was created Earl of Elgin. His son, early in the reign of Charles 1., was created Baron Bruce of Whorlton, in the English Peerage. Whorlton, in , the North Riding, and the dissolved Cistercian Abbey Jerveaux (Urevale), had been granted by Henry VIII. to the Earl of Lennox, but subsequently reverted to the Crown, and is said to have been regranted by James I. to Edward Bruce of Kinloss. The second wife of the second Earl of Elgin was the widow of the Earl of Oxford, and the daughter of the elder Cecil. According to one account, the Bruce 3 had large grants from King James of lands at Tanfield and elsewhere in Yorkshire, at one time in the possession of the Marmions ; but there is evidence to show that the elder Cecil had previously received a grant of these lands from Elizabeth; consequently, they must have been brought into tie family by the marriage with Cecil's daughter. Whichever account be true, they were derived by the direct favour of the Crown, whether of Elizabeth or James matters little. The eldest son of this marriage was crmted Earl of Anesbury. The next heir made a most for- tunate matrimonial alliance, his wife being the sister and sole heiress of William Seymour, Duke of Somerset, one of the wealthiest nobles in the kingdom. It is unnecessary here to recapitulate the history of the Seymours. Suffice it to say that one of them had married the daughter and co-heiress of Sir William Sturmy, of Chadham and Wolf Hall, in Wiltshire. The Sturmys from the days of Henry 11., had been hereditary Bailiffs of the Royal Forest of Sevemake, where is now situated Tottenham Park, the chief seat of the Marquis of Ailes- bury. This is only another instance of the tendency of hereditary guardianship to develop into ownership. The Protector Somerset in the reign of Edward VI. obtained— or,, rather, appropriated to himself—immense grants of land belonging to the Crown, which, however, he was ulti- mately compelled to disgorge. Marlborough dastle, Bradon, and Savernake Forests, and other lands derived from his ancestors, were re-stored to him. The present Marquis of Ailesbury owns in Wiltshire 37,993 acres. Yorkshire. 15,502 „ 1,565 „
Total —55,061 „ With a rent-roll of D59,716.* It will be seen from the forming account that nearly all this has been derived et varlom times by grants from the Crown.

The Earl of Aileslutry, whose marriage resulted (ii tiv3 acqUisitlod of the hey ir.4?lr estates, played a half-hetuted part at the Revolution of DM. He Wl9 one of the first invite the Prince of Oratigc over, but he resolutely refused to swear allegiance to him as King. als son married Lady Anne Saville, daughter and co-heiress of the Marquis of Halifax; but the Saville property passed to her daughter, and, as there were no male children, the Bari of Ailesbury obtained a new patent of peerage as Baron Bruce of Totten- ham, with remainder too a nephew, to whom he bequeathed his estates.

The Earldom of Ailesbury then expired, and the Scottish Earldom of Elgin passed to the Earl of Kincardine, who was descended from a brother of Edward Bruce of Kinloss, the courtier of James I. The tivo earldoms have been since held by his descendants, some of whom have achieved distinction in the public service. The seventh Earl, who was Ambassa- dor at Constantinople, brought home the "Elgin Marbles" from Greece, and the eighth Earl was not many years ago Governor-General of India.

The nephew, Thomas Brudenell, was a younger son of the Earl Of Cardigan. The Brudenells were small land- owners in Oxon and Northampton in the time of the Plantagenets. One of them, who was Lord Chief Justice in the reigns of Henry VII. an,l Henry VIII., mad.! considerabl.t •,:lichases of an at Staunton Wyvill, it: Leiceiter6hire, and Dectie, in North:ll;ptonshire, the latter place being the

chief seat of the family. One of his descendants received a baronetcy from James 1., and had a peerage from Charles I. Lord Brudenell was a staunch Royalist, and suffered a long imprisonment in the Tower, for which he was com- pensated at the Restoration by being created Earl of Cardi- gan. The eldest son of the second Earl of Cardigsn, who died in the lifetime of his father, married Lady Frances Saville, daughter of the Earl of Sussex, who subsequently became heiress to her brother's estates. These Savilles according to Allen's History of Yorkshire, were an illegi- timate branch of the family, who, by address and Court favour, had outstripped the legitimate line. Their lands are situated in Yorkshire. The grandson of the Saville marriage l rose to a dukedom, for, having married the co- heiress of the Duke of Montagu he was, after the death of his father-in-law, created Duke of Montagu. He died with- out issue, and his next brother succeeded to the Earldom of Cardigan, which continued to be held by the Brudenells till 1868, when the last Earl—he who led the Light Brigade at the charge of Balaclava—died without issue, and the Earl- dom of Cardigan passed to the Marquis of Ailesbury. The late Earl of Cardigan held in— ..
Northampionshire 6,313 acres. -York Leicester

Total 12,981 „ with a rent-roll of £16,130 What will be .the ultimate disposition of these lands I am unable to say. In the new Domesday Book they are set down as held by the trustees of the late Earl, whose widow resides at Deene, the old seat of the Brudenell family. In 1821 the then Earl of Ailesbury, who had steadily used the family electoral influence for the Government, was raised a step in the Peerage, being created a Marquis. The first Reform Bill swept away most of the Parliamentary influence of the Brudenell Braces, but they still have one representative in the House of Commons, who nominally sits for the little borough of Marlborough. The present Marquis, as Lord Ernest Bruce, sat for that place from 1832 till his accession to the Peerage in 1873. Marl- borough has barely 600 electors, while several boroughs, which also return only one member, have more than ten times that number. 'Among these are Swansea, Bury Burnley, Dewsbury, Dudley, Walsall, Gateshead, South Shields, Stockton, Huddersfield, and Wednesbury. The last- named has more than thirty-times the number of electors 'possessed by Marlborough: the contrast is a beautiful example of our electoral anomalies.
TI p present Lord Aberdare, Henry Austin Bruce, belongs to a Welsh family, he being the second son of Mr J. Bruce- Pryce, of Glaraorganshire.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.
ALLEGED CONSPIRACY TO MURDER 1110 11 OFFICIALS.

A vigorous raid has been made by the Dublin police, consequent, it is believed, on the information elicited at the prolonged private investigation ‘vhich has been going on at Dublin Castle for some weeks past. It is alleged that a for- midable conspiracy has been discovered, the object of which is to murder certain officials of the Irish Government and some members of the Dublin police force, and warrants 1 were accordingly issued for the arrest of 22 persons who are believed to be implicated in this plot. At a very early hour on Saturday morning the police set about the execu- tion of these warrants, and in the course of a few hours succeeded in arresting 17 of the persons of whom they were in search. Amongst these was Mr. James Carey, who was previously confined in Kihnainham as a suspect; and was, after his release, elected a member of the Dublin City Council. The whole of the prisoners appeared at the Northern._ Divisional Police Court on Saturday, and were there charged with conspiring with other per- sons "to murder certain public officers of the Govern- ment and others." No evidence was given beyond the formal informations of the officers upan which the arrests had been made, and the prisoners were then remanded for a week without bail.—On .eaturday evening another raid was made by the Dublin police in strong force. A number of public-houses were very closely searched, and the occupants subjected to close inspection, but though the raid extended over about an hour no further arrests were made. Dublin was outwardly quite calm and orderly while these exciting proceedings were in progress, and though crowds gathered round the houses that were being visited there was in no case any attempt to create a disturbance. Conflicting opinions prevail as to the value of the present arrests, but on the whole the public, remenibering previous abortive proceedings, are not disposed to think that the present prosecutions will lead to any extraordinary revelations. The police, however, though very reticent, regard the arrests as matters of the first importance.—ln Dublin, on Monday, the arrests continued to excite public attention, which was 1 further stimulated by the apprehension of three of the five persons whom the police failed to arrest on Saturday. The prisoners were formally charged with conspiracy, and were remanded until Saturday. A seizure of rifles and ammunition was also made in Patrick-street, near Christ Church Cathedral, and it is also said that important docu- ments have fallen into the hands of the police. A correspondent writes :—" There are rumours afloat to the effect that at least four informers will be put into the witness box, and that the revelations to be made will occupy the magistrates some weeks. I have as yet no definite in- formation on the subject, but according to general report the evidence will be given on the part of the Crown of the existence of the secret organisation in Dublin, and appro- vers will be produced with a view of showing that they belonged to it, that some of them were present when assassi- nations were discussed, and that they were actually assigned to participate in the murders. Detectives will he examined to testify that for the past two years they have been employed on special political duty watching men suspected of or known to belong to illegal societies ; that they have closely observed their movements, have known them to atteml private meetings held in stale, garrets, and back I lanes, the utmost secrecy being observed t and that they have seen some of the prisoners attend such meetings. They will be examined to prove that they have seen some of the prisoners in company, and apparently in consultation, in places notoriously frequented by men who either have been convicted, or are now awaiting trial, charged with mur- derous outrages or attempted assassinations. An effort will be made to prove that on the date of the Dorset-street murder some of the accused had been in the company of those actually pasted in a certain part of the city for the purpose of assassinating a high Government official, but that the chances being unfavourable to the attempt it was abandoned for a better opportunity, which, as regarded the intended victim, fortunately never arose. It is said that it will be shown there was a plot at one time to destroy the Viceroy and his escort by means of bombs to be thrown from unoc- cupied dwellings or houies in course of construction. -It is eged that circumstances will be detailed as to how the murderers were decided on, the reasons given, and the selede tion of the perpetrators made, the latter being responsible with their own lives for carrying out the decrees by means only known to themselves. Evidence will be forthcoming of the storage and discovery of arms in Dublin, and the seizures made from time to time. It is expected that further arrests will be !glade."

The Daily News learns that a large number of labourers in the West of Ireland have expressed a desire to emigrate to Queensland, and steps will he taken to ascertain the views of the Colonial °ince on the matter.

The Queen's Bench, on Monday, refused a conditional order sought by Mr. O'Brien, editor of United Ireland, directing the police magistrate to take evidence as to the truth of the statements in the incriminated article headed "Accusing spirits." Mr. O'Brien is, therefore, returned for trial on a charge of publishing a seditious libel. A package of dynamite was discovered the other evening in one of the receivers of the Limerick Post-office. It was laid aside by the clerk who took it during the work of stamping, and before anything further was done in connec- tion with it, suspicion was aroused, and it was opened. The Postmaster has made inquiry into the matter. It appears that several clerks handled the explosive without suspicion of danger, and that a letter-carrier named Sullivan first detected its real nature. The dynamite weighed three ounces. The police have obtained no clue. Shortly before one on Tuesday morning, an attack was made on two constables, on duty at the South Circular-road, Dublin, by a number of young men said to be medical students. The police had interfered to check a disturbance which had arisen, when they were assailed so violently that one of them drew his revolver and threatened to fire. A , desperate struggle ensued for possession of the revolver. Two soldiers interfered to protect the police, and, with the kelp of a reinforcement of constables, four rioters were arrested.

Patrick Higgins was executed on Monday morning in Galway County Prison for complicity in the murder of the Huddys, bailiffs of Lord Ardilaun. The weather was bois- terous, and few people assembled outside. Higgins met his doom with great firmness, and died very quickly, being a heavy and powerful man. On Wednesday morning, the two remaining convicta who participated in the Lough Mask tragedy—Thomas Higgins and Michael Flynn—were hanged in Galway Prison. They made no statement, and walked with apparent firmness to the scaffold, where they died almost instantly.

LATCIIFORD TRITE BLUES (FIRST). —These ebbs met on the ground of the former, on Saturday last, and after about half an hour's fast play the visitors secured a try, which was contested into a goal. Stu:fly after half-time was called, when the home team had the wind in their favour, and in ten minutes' fast play the home team gained two tries and one goal. The visitors, seeing that the home team was winning easily, left the field in a most disgraceful manner, which we hope never to see again. The tries for Latchford were obtained by Wright, Henshaw, and Acton, the former kicking, the goal. Latchford team: Back, Hough; three- quarter backs T. Bargess and A Jones; half-backs, G. H. WIDNES.—These clubs met for the first time at Middleton-road Cheetham Hill. on Saturday. The home team was much weakened by the absence of the two three quarterbacks, Holt and Flower, besides Wilkes, Blyton, and A Flower, forwards. Their places were efficiently filled by Heap and Sheriff. The visitors had likewise left two or three promi7ent men behind; they revertheries mat-le a. good stand, and after a very fast game the Hiii men had the advantage by one goal, one try, and several minor points, to one goal and some half dozen minor points. The gcal for the home team was dropped by Sheriff after a good run, and the try was ob- tained by Poison, Mark failing at the place. The try for Widnes was the result of a sharp piece of play by 'Tamil, Morris doing the honours from a difficult position. The game throughout was very fairly contested. WARRINGTON V. BT. HELENS RECREATION (tar TMs) These clubs met for the second time this season, at it. Helens. on Saturday. The weather was bitterly cold and the field almost ankle deep in mud, making good play very difficult. The Warringtonians were disappointed of the services of two of their usual back players. Bt. He'ens, on the other hand, had whipped together the best team they have played for some time. The St.'Helens captain won the t.:lls, and elected to de. fend the pavilion goal. . F. Turner kicked off in a downpour of rain. The ret.urn was good, and the " Saints " for some time had the best of the game, getting well into their oppo- nents' 25. Here the ball was passed to Cunliffe (the Saints' half-back), who was unsuccessfully tackled by Buxton, Walsh, and J Turner in succession, and eventually planted the ball behind the goal posts. The place kick resulted in a goal. The Becreaticnists still had the best of the game, registering two touchdowns shortly after. The Warrington forwards now be- gan to work together with a will, a combined nosh taking the ball within 15 yards of their opponents' goal line. Buxton got the leather from a line out and .dropped a, beautiful goal amid tiernendous cheers. The remainder of the play was almost entirely in neutral territory, Cualiffe and Seddon occasionally breaking away, but always embracing "mother earth "before going many yards, the embrace, by the way, not being very warm under the circumstances. Barnes at one time was conspicuous by a very smart collar. At the call of time it was found that the game had ended in a draw, War- rington having scored one goal. St. Helens, one goal and two touchdowns. The visitors' forwards played a remarkably good game, but their efforts were neutralised by the home backs, who, on the whole, were superior to the opposing backs. The Warrington team was as follows :—J Turner, full back f T Walsh and T Barnes, three-quarter backs; J 111 Warren (captain) and J Buxton. half-Nacks ; F Turner, W Fovey, H Ashton, T Knowles, J Boardman, J Isherwood, F Hughes, C Rimmer, J Rigby, and another, forwards.

RUNCORN V. ITALIMEN —This mttch was played at Runcorn on Saturday. Grundy kicked off, Wilkinson headisig the ball back. Joule followed up and got pis.essien. but on Mullen tackling him he passed to Lewis, who kicked into Marsh's hands, that player exchanging kicks with Larkin. Prescott and Rushton then dribbled well, Wright and Atherton re- sponding in good style. Harper punted into Runcorn territory, where a scrimmage or two ended in H. Hughes getting away, and J. B. Clarke being s3en to advantage. Wright as next In possession, and after giving a lot of trouble was brought down by Norbury. Wilkinson and J. Clarke were well to the front, and Johnson further improved the situation. Grundy punted nicely into Runoorn's twenty-five, and a bit of good dribbling by Harper.and Gardiner enabled the latter player to score. Grundy kicking a neat goal. Wright re-started the game. and Hi:Maud was instrumental In getting the ball into Walkden's quarters. Here the game was hotly contested, and Andrews; who is always dangerous on the goal line, ran in. Mason's kick at goal was, however, too low. Athert,n returned the drop out, which NNW neutralized by Bagulley. Half time was now called. Prescott returned the kick o/, when Johnson eluded several players, and almost got behind. Wright, Atherton, and Joule kept the ball in the enemy's camp, and Hughes tried hard to score. Harper and Norbury worked the ball back to neutral ground. Wright was again to the front, the ball falling Into the hands of Harper, who was collared by Atherton. Gatley here gained ground, which H. Hughes further improved, and Wright, handing off all opposi- tion, gained a try. which Mason converted into a goal, amidst great cheering. Wainwright returned effectively to the kick- off, and Larkin and Mason replied to punts by Grundy and Marsh. flatley and Joule got the ball back again to the quarter flag, where Andrews secured the oval and scored another try, Mason again scoring the major point. Grandy shortly afterwards made a grand attempt to drop a goal, the ball rebounding from the uprights. div.p: THE MEMBERS FOR SOUTH-WEST • LANCASHIRE AND THEIR CON- STITUINTS.

Sir R. A. Cross and Colonel Ireland Blackburne, the members for South-West Lancashire, were present on Wed- nesday evening at a demonstration in the Cambridge Hall, Southport, in connection with the Soutieport and Birkdale Conservative Clubs. There were many hundreds of people present, the handsome hall being crewded to its utmost capacity. Mr. H.L. Gregory presided .The Chairman, after some preliminary observations, introduced Colonel Ireland Blackburne, M.P., who was loudly cheered, and who returned thanks for the enthusiastic reception accorded to him. He said that although in the House of Commons defeats had been sustained by the Conservative party--- defeats admittedly on account of overwhelming numbers— still there was not a man in their ranks who need be ashamed of the occurrence after the election of 1880. (Cheers.) Referring to the cloture, the speaker said it was owing to Mr. Gladstone's eloquence and representation that the House was unable to cope with the business of the country, and that some politicians and moderate thinkers arrived at the conclusion that it was desirable to have the cloture, which meant indeed the suppression of fair, legitimate, and just debate. Speaking of Egypt, he said there ought to have been no war if the Government had acted with firmness in their policy. (Cheers.)_ Sir R. A. Cross referred to the subject of Egypt. He deprecated either leaving the country hastily or annexing it, holding that we should not leave it until matters were settled on a firm and sound basis. With regard to Ireland he said much of the loss of life and property in that country, much of the feeling raised of class against class, and much of the disloyalty to the Crown might have been prevented if -the Government had only rigorously carried out the measures placed at their disposal. As to intended reforms, he urged an attitude of watchfulness on the part of the Conservatives.

THE MILES PLATTING CASE.—Dean Cowie, Canon Knox- Little, and other clergymen of the diocese have addressed a remarkable letter to the Bishop of Manchester in regard to the Miles Platting difficulty. They entreated the Bishop to consider "the desirableness of peace," and suggest that a "wise and charitable policy of live and let live" would remove existing hindrances to peace. They suggest that if" strict law" is to be enforced all round" the strain may be too severe for the safety of the Church."

MR. BRADLAUGH'S FUTURE ACTION. Mr. Bradlaugh, M.P., announces that he.shall not further proceed with action Bradlaugh v. Erskine. *12.1i1 arose out of '.llli endea- vour to take his seat in. House: T.'ne bon. member, in a letter annoutt-;,g his decision, says that "many people in tie country think and say even now that he is excluded to hinder him from proceeding with the attack on the pension list." He suggests to those who have any care for the dignity of Parliament "that even if the wearisomeness and cost of the struggle should in the end cripple him, a victory so gained will be a loss to'Parliamentary prestige of serious character." He knows how h4rl it is in a contest for either to give way, and would remind all "how easily a golden bridge might have been found by the passing of an Affirma- tion Bill." The further complications of the struggle are not easy to foresee. Member for Northampton, it is his right and his duty to take his seat. He shall try to exercise his right and perform his duty. A case which came before the Birmingham bench on Monday, in which a so-called astrologer was remanded one eharge of fraudulent advertising, showed that an astounding amount of credulity prevails, and drew from the presiding Magistrate an expression of surprise that "so many fools Could be found in the kingdom." A CorrEmPTIBLE Timm—The box displayed at Bangor ILailway Station for the reception of subscriptions in aid of the Clio industrial training ship was on Monday discovered to have been wrenched from its fastenings and carried

. _ I"Way. Subsequently it was found in a closet, haying been Btcashed open, and the contents, less 2d, stolen. The action for breach of promise of marriage brought by a Medical man named Kingsley against a Dublin lady named Piele has ended in favour of the defendant. The ittrY gave the plaintiff a farthing damages in respect of the breach of promise, but found for the lady on her counter- claim for £lOO for money lent. The report that Miss Piele Was Mr. Kingsley's senio, by 15 years was an error. She is a Year or two his junior, and her age is 36. The prisoner ‘tted he collected the money, but said he intended , Day it over to the committee by whom ha was author- used. He was fined £5, or in default one month's imprison- Inen t. _

CLEVER ESCAPE OF A CoNvicr.—A convict named Jos. Nealbam, convicted at Shrewsbury in 1881 of burglary, and sentenced to fifteen years' penal servitude, escaped from Pertsea Convict Prison early on Monday morning. The convict made a hole in the ceiling, and having gained the Prison roof, slid down the spouting. dropped into an adjoin- ing court, and made for the open country. He was there .!een by a policeman, who gave chase, but became ex- causted, and returned to Portsmouth to telegraph the escape In all directions. The convict was recaptured on Tuesday .a.f tern 00 n . He was attired as a clergyman, and at first _ _

_ threatened his pursuer with a knife. Being exhausted with hunger and fatigue, however, he eventually submitted. EXTRAORDINARY CASE OF MISTAKEN IDENTITY.—A Most extraordinary case of mistaken identity came before the county magistrates at Manchester, on Tuesday. Edward vrowder, solicitors' clerk, who had been employed by two of the principal firms in Manchester, and who was now in the employ of solicitors practising in court, was charged with burglary and assaulting the police. A quantity of wearing ...apparel had been stolen and hidden, and Police-constable alaxwell was appointed to watch it. He asserted that at Midnight Crowder and a woman weje removing the pro- Deny, when be seized Crowder, who called upon the woman to get a trick, with which he knocked him insensible. A large number of witnesses, including Crowder's employer, were called to prove that he could not possibly have been the man; and the officer, who still asserted he was, said he had known him three years. The magistrates, believing it Was a case of mistaken identity, discharged Crowder. THE NEW LAW COURTS.—Neither judges, barristers, nor 'Witnesses are enamoured of the uew law courts. Draughts, darkness, inability to boar, and other discomforts are complained of, and on Saturday a witness who had left his overcoat on a bookcase when he entered the witness-box dis- covered that it had been stolen when he returned to search for it. This little incident was not due to any fault of the builders or designers, and it may be hoped that sliding _ _ _ _ . .

seats and desks-which allow their contents to slip down CO the floor may be found not difficult to remedy. Acoustic defects, however, may be of a more troublesome character, though it may be hoped that Mr. Justice Watkin Williams's doctrine of patience may produce good results. _ LORD DERBY A'ND LORD S,EETON AT LIVERPOOL. On Saturday night the Earl of Sefton, President of the Liver- Pool Reform Club, gave a reception in that building in com- memoration of the recent Liberal victory in the city elec- tion, and also of the elevation of Lord Derby, a member of the club, to a seat in the Cabinet. The reception commenced at nine o'clock, and the guests were met by Lord and Lady Sefton, and a party from Croxteth Hall. Lord and Lady Derby, Lady Margaret Cecil, and others from Knowsley Rall were also present; and the company included Mr. S. Smith, M.P., the newly-elected member for Liverpool ; Sir Thotnas Earle, Sir Jamee Picton, Mr. S. Williamson, M.P., Mr. John Roberts, M.P., and Mr. W. S. Caine, M.P. All the members of the club, numbering nearly 900, were invited, and the attendance was very numerous. Representatives of the Manchester Reform Club and of Liberal clubs in Liver- Pool were present. The invitations were extended to ladies, and there was a very brilliant gathering. The occasion formed an effective termination to Mr. Arthur E trle's tenure of the office of chairman of the club. Arr. DATITT AT OLDHAM. Mr. Devitt met with a very unfriendly reception at Oldham on Saturday night. As soon as he appeared on the platform at the Co-operative da Ila body of men arose and vowed their determination bat he should not be heard. These were not Englishmen, ut Irish "Nationalists," who are supposed to have been fended by some of Mr. Davitt's utterances. They stormed be platform, and a perfect melee ensued, in which sticks nd bludgeons and fragments of furniture were used to the erious injury of several persons. Mr. Devitt spoke of the isturbers in very unflattering terms; and declared several lines that with twenty men he could clear the room of .hem. He became 'eTeatly excited, and the police thought necessary to warn him that if he did not keep quiet he ba taken to the Town Hall. Finally the policemen tjected the " Nationalists,"—" handling them out," says the tePort," neck and crop." During an interval of compara- kive quiet Mr. Devitt managed to sky a few words. What a 'Peetacle, he remarked, for the English people to look upon! They were asking for self-government from England, and hese were the men who would dare to govern Ireland and :Ile her destinies! THREAT TO MURDER A VACCINATION-OFFICER.—During 1 the hearing of a case on Monday at the Hyde Police Court, M which two persons named North and Cooke were sum- I .....reoned for neglecting to comply with the provisions of the I vaccination Act, the magistrates' clerk read the following letter, which bad been received by the vaccination-officer Or the district. It was addressed "E. U. Taylor, Bredbury, near Stockport." --• "Hyde, January 1, 1883. Sir,—' Do Your duty and die.' When any vile and murderous law is Placed upon the statute-book of this country, there is always Liome earthly vagabond base enough to carry out that law. he Vaccination Acts are murdering helpless infants, and B°wing disease broadcast, and yet you are vagabond enough I :0 enforce them. The only way to deal with such scamps I is to put them out of existence,' and I hereby give you I notice that if you force me to have my child vaccinated, I will shoct you dead within forty-eight hours after the °De-ration is performed.' Ponder this over, and ask yourself fit would not be better to relinquish such a damnable course ef action. However, rest assured that I shall be as good as 1113' word, and I will take care that my revolver does not 111188 fire.—Yours, PRINCIPLE."—The reading of the letter caused considerable sensation in court. Mr. Wood, the Presiding magistrate, said he thought that course of action would not avail the Anti-Vaccination League, and might -13 to do their cause harm. Both defendants, as members c! the League, disclaimed any knowledge of the letter or its lathor, and said they would leave the Society at once if toirlY thought such a letter had emanated from any member The magistrates expressed the belief that it had not b_7o int.written by any member of the organisation, and the ?.ders haying been made in the two cases under considera- "en, the parties left the court.
