div.head: TIM EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 20, 1883
div.p: TIM EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 20, 1883
FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE,
A SHOCKING AFFAIR AT BIRKEN-
HEAD.

A shocking affair occurred in the express train from London to Birkenhead on Saturday night. It appears that when the train was passing through Bebington station a passenger heard the report of a firearm in an adjoining com- partment of the carriage. On the arrival of the train at Woodside, Birkenhead, he communicated nith the railway authorities, and in a second-class compartment was found the dead body of a man of gentlemanly appearance. He sat in an upright posture, and in his right hand he held a one-barrelled pistol of an old-fashioned pattern. He was disfigured past recognition. His face was almost completely blown off, and his brains were protruding from under the skull. His clothes were saturated with blood, and at the bottom of the 'carriage were pools of blood. The cushions of the carriage were also besmeared with blood. A medical gentleman was in attendance, and pronounced life to be ex- tinct. The body was subsequently removed to the dead- house in Watson-street. The deceased, it is supposed, was about 35 years of age. He was sft:7in. in height, and had dark brown hair, which was beginning to turn grey. His chin was shaven, but he had side whiskers. He was clad in a black worsted suit, which did not appear to have been much worn. He also wore laced-up boots and brown stock- ings. He was of slight build. In his possession was found about £3 in gold and silver. Wrapped up in brown paper in one of his pockets was a quantity of powder, together with caps and slugs t® fit the pistol with which, it is sup- posed, he shot himself. No papers were found upon him which would give any clue to his identity; but from the fact that a small whisky bottle, labelled "Smith, White Lion Hotel, Foregate-street, Chester," was foun€l in his pos- session, it is supposed that he hailed from that town. An inquest was held on the body of deceased, which had not been identified on Monday, and the jury returned a verdict of "Committed suicide." The deceased was on Tuesday Identified as a local accountant named Gibson.

div.head: AN INDIAN OFFICER'S IMPRESSIONS
div.p: AN INDIAN OFFICER'S IMPRESSIONS
OF ENGLAND.

One of the native officers who recently visited England fprnishes the following account of his impressions to an Indian paper :—" Being a native of India, and having never before left it, I, of course, had no real idea what England was, although I had heard a great deal about it, its people, the wondrous things, and great workshops there. After the campaign in Egypt; it became known that certain of us were tojkisit the great country of which ours is a depen- dency Tnd when I was selected I became very glad, a feeling of pride possessed me, and I prayed that God would long continue the reign of Her Most Gracious Majesty the Queen. The others who were selected were also very glad, and until the day of our landing we speculated variously as to what was to be seen. We went first te Liverpool, then by rail to London. Everywhere we were heartily cheered, and the people seemed to know of our coming. We all con- sider London to be number one place in the world; we do not think there could be another city in the world to equal it. We never saw such crowds as were present at the re- view of the troops by the Queen. We fully appreciate the kindness of her Majesty in pinning with her own hands the medals on our breasts, but she soiled her bands by touching us—we are too insignificant for her to touch. She inspected us at Buckingham Palace, touched our swords, and said a few kind and encouraging words to us. On one occasion we went to see the Duke of Buckingham, who received us very cordially, and gave us an opportunity of witnessing a little sport. Ten or twelve gentlemen, attended by about twenty hounds, formed a hunting party, and caught a fox, while we looked on. Never did we see such a great bear as the ' Polar bear in the Zoological Gardens. He seemed warm, while we were shivering with cold. The National Gallery, Westminster Abbey, the Houses of Parliament, and every place of note,were seen by us; but I think, and my comrades agree with me, that nothing beats the Crystal Palace. 1 We all consider it the handsomest building in London, and , Windsor Castle comes next. What most took our fancy in the Crystal Palace was the picture of a battle in the Franco- German war. Everything in it looked like life. We prefer it to the pictures in the National Gallery. It is the best picture in London. We liked the theatres and circuses, especially the latter, for the wonderful feats of horseman- ship and strength which were displayed. Many preferred seeing the performances of the dancing girls, but we did not care much for the ballet. One day two men and myself went to Brighton to see Colonel Campbell, commanding our regiment. Brighton is very beautiful ; I liked it better than London, aid could live there for ever. We have seen more wonderful things than we thought of. Almost every thing was number one. The women are pretty, the men brave and hospitable, and the country such that we do not think there is another like it. Unfortunately, only two of us could speak English; but none were inconvenienced in any way; and we could not have been better attended to."

THE OPERATIONS OF THE SALVATION ARMY. Addressing an influential meeting held at the head- quarters of the Salvation Army, Queen Victoria-street, London, on Saturday, General Booth said that there were no signs of the Army losing its charm or power ever the multitude. Travelling as he did all over the country, he assured his hearers that the Army was an organisation of as deep interest to the maases of thp people as ever it had proved to ,)a before. In London alone, with thb exception of a few meeting places in remote corners of the city, every building the Army possessed was crowded to excess every Sunday, and notably so was the Clanton Congress Hall and the Grecian Theatre, or " Eagle," from which latter place 400 converts lately marched out in procession. This procession included converted thieves, infidels, drunk- ards, criminals, and Bradlaughites. At Clanton the Army was similarly successful. It had now 455 corps and 1,095 officers, being an increase of 129 and 335 respect- , ively since August last. It had satisfactorily established itself in Paris, where it had a good fighting corps and crowded congregations. The mo%ement had successfully extended to Switzerland. To New Zealand two officers were despatched the preceding day. From India there was a call for reinforcements, and a new detachment was about to be sent thither. Reverting to Switzerland, he said that country was regarded as a favourable ground for operating upon Italy, Germany, and France. Operations in Australia were self-supporting, the Army's pioneer there landing at Melbourne without almost a penny in his pocket. Good news, too, had been received of the progress of the Army in Sweden, Canada' and the United States. In India natives were joining the Army, one of whose officers had been welcomed by a Prince of Delhi, and one of the leading Maharajahs said, "If the Salvation Army cannot do any good for India nobody can." Major Tucker after prosperously establishing the move- ment in Calcuttz, had gone to Madras, where Christians we heipiAg him onward. The world was before them, aid God "wpm their side. When funds allowed a detachment would "procee3 to the Cape forthwith. Towards the pur- chase of the Clapton and Eagle properties friends last year contributed 03,000. To keep things afloat at head-quarters and throughout the country £4OO per week was needed. In order to make up a deficiency of £B,OOO in the Eagle pur- chase money eight gentlemen lent £l,OOO each for twelve months. Property had been bought all over the country, but he did not think they had any reason to fear financially if their friends would only help the Army to the extent they had hitherto done. If they did, the Army would not be sold up or bothered with bailiffs. Seeing that the annual income of the London City Mission was £IO,OOO, he did not think that £20,000 a year to carry OR the extensive and far-reaching work af the Salvation Army was an exorbitant sum to ask for. Speeches commending the movement to public support were then made by Mr. Commissioner Rail ton, Mrs. BoetAßev. T. M. Humphreys, a clergy- man of the Churc ngland, and others; and the pro- ceedings closed with prayer.

AN ENGLISH REVOLUTIONARY MANIFESTO. It was announced in the papers the other day that Liver- pool and other provincial towns are about to receive a " visitation " from some members of an organisation calling itself "The English National Revolutionary League." Louise Michel, the notorious French Socialist, is also likely to visit the provinces in connection with the League. Some light is thrown on the mission of this body in a letter from its president, Mr. Charles W. Oldham, who very candidly explains what he and his fellow-revolutionaries are working for. Mr. Oldham writes:—"Few people in this country appear to know the ideas: of,Socialists, or to comprehend .what the Social Revolution really is to be. Speaking in the name of the English Revolutionary League, I may say that we consider that the present conditions of society, in which the unfairly rich oppress the poor, and where the strong tyran- nise over the weak, highly unsatisfactory, unnaturale and calculated to bring about the complete degradation and, slavery of the most important section of humanity. W, aim, therefore, at revolutionising the present condition of society. We intend to upset existing institutions and forms of government which do, not give expression to the will and are opposed to the welfare of the people; and to bring about a new and happier condition of society where monarchs, priests, and thrones will be no more, where crime and tyranny no more can live, and where an ennobled and enlightened humanity will work together for the general welfare and the public good, in place of an insane worship of an unknown deity and a useless king. Kings and priests, , altars and thrones, crowns and mitres, 'we regard as the emblems of tyranny and force and fraud in every land and every clime; and we look forward to the time when they shall be swept away nevermore to torment and tyrannise over human kind." The president of the Revolutionary League' having spoken thus far about his doctrines, proceeds to discuss the means by which they are to be brought into practice. He is not inclined to be " squeamish " about these weans, but he does not advocate an immediate and general armed "rising." The president then elaborates his views on the subject of assassi- nation, which, he maintains, is a fairly debatable theme. "I assert (says Mr. Oldham) that there are circumstances under which political assassination is not only justifiable but necessary, and that there are times when so-called , • leurder 'is no crime. Where you have a tyrant grinding down his heel upon the people as though they were not of human kind; where you have a despot crushing and • oppressing humanity, causing the loss of innocent lives floading a country with blood, and filling its dungeons with prisoners who have dared to protest against his arbitrary will—l say to assassinate that man is no murder ' and can

be no crime. It is useless to disguise the fact that this is the real secret underlying revolutionary success ; and the history of the world proves that my theory is correct— namely, that political assassination, discreetly carried out, is necessary for the welfare, the advancement, and the prosperity of human kind."

div.head: – TERRIBLE DISASTER IN RUSSIA.
div.p: - TERRIBLE DISASTER IN RUSSIA.
OVER 300 LIVES LOST.

News from St. Petersburr states that on Saturday night, whilst a performance was being given in a circus at Berdit- scheff, a commercial town of Russian Poland, in the govern- ment of Kieff, a fire broke out, and before the spectators could escape, the whole building was in flames, and it is estimated over three hundred persons perished. The town of Berditscheff is the Polish Berdyczoo and is situated in Russian Poland, in the government of Kieff. It is a place of considerable importance as a com- mercial centre. It has a resident population of 50,000, but this number is largely increased on the occasion of the quarterly fairs, when the city is visited by dealers from a long distance, chiefly Austrian, and a very large business is done. It is probable that the visit of the circus was on the occasion of one of these fairs, so that the loss of over 300 lives may include those of many visitors covering a very large-district of that part of the Continent. The resident population is largely composed of Jews, and pilgrimages are also made to the church of a large Carmelite Convent in the town from all parts of Russia. Russia is visited by English circus companies, and Continental companies often comprise many leading English equestrian performers. - Berditscheff is about twenty miles south of Jitomir, which is about sixty miles from Kieff. A St. Petersburg correspondent gives the following details :—" The fire was caused by a lamplighter upsetting a, lighted lamp in the stables, the flames from which com- municated with a barrel of petroleum. - Tne whole building appeared to be in a blaze instantly, the fire running from the stables to the ether portions with alarming rapidity. A performance was proceeding at the time, many of the audience being workpeople and mechanics. Directly the fire was noticed a panic seized upon the people. There was an instantaneous rush for the doors, with the inevitable consequence that the exits became blocked directly. Those behind made frantic struggles to reach the outer air, scramb- ling over the heads of those in front, and in the crush many were suffocated, while others sank under the tremendous pressure and were trampled to death. The heartrending shrieks of the unfortunate victims as they fought their way produced tbe most intense excitement among the townspeople, who rapidly flocked to the scene. But only a few minutes appeared to have elapsed before the flames encircled the whole circus, and it was evident that those who had not effected their escape were doomed. The burning oil in escaping from the petroleum cask in the stable had run towards the main building, carrying a living stream of fire, and adding to the inflammable material of which the circus was composed. To the shrieks and groans of the human sufferers were added the terrified cries from the horses in the building as they were gradually roasted to death. All the animals in the circus were burnt to death, and this will give some idea of the rapidity with which the flames spread. Some of the audience, by the aid of those outside, were able to effect their escape, but these were comparatively few. Nine of those who obtained their freedom after the most strenuous exertions, did so at the expense of injuries to themselves. One of these has since died from the effects of his wounds, and some of the others are lying in a critical state. On Sunday,an attempt was made to recover the bodies of those who had perished, and this work has continued ever since. The terrible sights which have been revealed are sickening in their horror. At the main entrance to the circus lay the burnt and blackened bodies of a heap of victims, their heads fairly outside the door, while their bodies are held as though in a vice by those who crushed upon them from behind. Further inside the ruins many of the bodies were burnt to a cinder. Others who had been crushed down early in the struggle, and were buried beneath a mass of human beings, preserved sufficient of the features to afford easy means of identification, but in nearly all cases the aspect of the victims was fearful to look upon. As each body was taken from the ruins it was placed in a tempo- rary mortuary, there to await the recognition of friends. Here, again, the scenes were such as to fairly baffle descrip- tion, the dreadful appearance of some of the bodies causing relatives the most acute suffering. The corpses, which it was impossible to identify from the terrible nature of their injuries, have been interred in the cemetery belonging to the Orthodox National Church. It was a very painful and impressive ceremony, the most affecting feature being that - many of those present who were deploring their lost friends were very probably assisting at the obsequies of their own relatives without being aware of it. The Vienna correspondent of the Daily Chronicle gives the following account of the catastrophe :—" The perform- ance had reached the fifth item in the programme, some clowns being in the ring, when another clown in acting costume rushed in, shouting" Fire !" At first the people

thought this was Part of the performance, and laughed but immediately afterwards the ringmaster rushed in and gave the alarm. The scene of horror that ensued was in- describable. The audience were so closely packed that motion was' almost impossible. Some in despair flung themselves from the galleries, and parents unable to save themselves made a desperate attempt to save their children by throwing them down into the ring. Some of the men, wear- ing the long coats of the Russian Jews, were entangled on spikes, and remained hanging in the air, while the whole building resounded with heartrending cries. In the ring, where the clowns had been performing, there was a carpet, and for a little while the children were safe in the centre of this; but when the grown-up people in their des- pair began jumping from the dress circle and galleries, the whole ring" became one inextricable mass, in which the children were trampled to death or suffocated before the flames reached them. But even this was not the worst. The horses soon became unmanageable, and about ,a dozen of them, driven ;nad with pain and terror, broke into the ring, trampling to death the people huddled together there. All this occurred in less time than it takes to describe, aud in twenty minutes all was over—at least half the people who had been in the building being burned to death or suffocated. At the windows and various exits scenes of the most horrible description were enacted, some of the strongest, in their efforts to extricate themselves from the struggling mAss, forcing others weaker than themselves into the flames."

It is naw ascertained that the number of persons who perished by the burning of the hotel at Milwaukee is 82. Count von Moltke is obliged to keep his room owing to a slight cold. No danger, however, is apprehended from the attack. It is reported from Scutari that rich mines of iron and coal have been discovered in the mountain near F:ulati, in Albania. - - -

Sir A. Colvin, according to a telegram from Alexandria is to be appointed Financial Adviser ef the Egyptian Minister of Finance. The remains of the late M. Gambetta were consigned to the family vault at Nice on Saturday, amidst demonstra- tions of popular admiration for the deceased and regret for his loss. _ _ _

Intelligence from Arthena, in the province of Murcia, states that seven shocks of earthquake occurred there on the 11th inst. There was no loss of life, but the inhabitants are in a state of great alarm. It is observed that the French Pretenders have un- wittingly paid great homage to Gambetta, for no sooner does he die than they make a rush to offer themselves to France, as though to fill up the vacancy. The police of Rome made domiciliary visits to more than 100 houses the other night, and arrested 125 persons and made a seizure of newspapers containing accounts of the life of Oberdank and his so-called martyrdom. " Conflicting " accounts of the reception of Cetewayo in Zululand have been received at Durban. A Times despatch states that the "haughty demeanour" of the King since the landing has been generally remarked. He tells all the people he meets that he dislikes the partition of the country. The other day a Caffre victory over the Boers of the Transvaal was announced. Following the custom which has been set in these cases, it is now stated that the " victory" was "the other way." The Boers defeated the Caffres, and.septurecl an important position. ROMANTIC AFFAIR INPARTs.--A terrible case of murder, and attempted suicide is chronicled from Paris. A butler named Million, in the house of a rich gentleman, M. Orsetti, in the Rue de Courcelles, fell in love with one of the housemaids, Marie, azd was engaged to be married to her. The other servants poked so much fun at Marie that she told Million she would have nothing more to do with him. He went to her room at night, and, not receiving a satisfactory answer to his suit, shot her dead through the heart. He afterwards shot himself through the chin, and lies at the Beaujon Hos- pital in a dangerous state. The Maori chiefs who lately visited Ervoand arrived a

the Bay of Islands on November 14. One a the chiefs has written to a friend in this country to inform him that the Ngapuhi chiefs were going to have a great meeting at the Treaty of Waitangi Hall, on Decembn 8 to receive from their countrymen a report of the results of their mission to England. The scheme for the settlement of the native land question in New Zealand which has been proposed by Lord Shaftesbury, the Bishop of London, Mr. Mundella, and other influential persons, was being eagerly discussed by the natives.

The courteous British Note which has been communicated to the Porte deals with the Egyptian judicial, financial, military, and general administrative systems, the changes and reforms required for securing to the people the greatest possible measure of sound government, the best means of guaranteeing order, tranquility, prosperity, and progress, and the regulations proposed to be made in reference to the Suez Canal. The Note was presented to the Egyptian Government immediately after its reception by the Porte. MANIFESTO BY PRINCE NAFOLEON.—Prince Napoleon (Jerome) has thought the present an oppOrtune time to remind France of his existence, and has accordingly issued a manifesto calling attention to the incompetence of the (Invernment, the disunion in Parliamentary parties, the diso" - ` •,, the national finances, and the danger to religion, which receivo nrotection from the State. He rejects any conipromise evalists is in favour of the Con- cordat, reminds France oi 6. ebiscitcs in favour of the Napoleonic *bile, and claims to no sole representative of that dynasty. The French Governme.... have arrested the Prince because of the issu of this manifesto, and on being taken before a court be has admitted the authorship of the document. His attach alon the Republican Govorn- ment is forc.ble, if somewhat botibastic, and the Ministry, by the promptitude of their action show the gravity which they attach to the proclamation. Political parties have been much excited by it, and it is Pissible that, following so closely upon the death of M. Gamietta, it may produce a unity among the various sections of Republicans which will not be without good effect.

div.head: AN OLD CRY REVIVED.
div.p: AN OLD CRY REVIVED.

The Duke of Rutland, writing from Be'wok Castle to the Times, says :—" I read your article with much alarm; and I wish to ask whether, in the opinion of the greater number of Englishmen,the time has not arrived when some endeavour should be made to save England, before it be too late, from her downward course. You say that the revenue is stagnant, if not declining ; that it is also difficult to escape from the conclusion that we may have to deal before long, with a period, more or less protracted, of restricted profits and con- sequent difficulties in trade. Competition has increased and is increasing in every branch of business, and the margin of profit is cut so close in consequence that there is a distinct diminution in the "staying power "of traders.' You also observe that in the most important branches of British com- merce we have been, of late, selling less, and on the whole at lower prices, than in 1881.' This, no doubt, is a very serious state of things, and should receive the careful consideration of every lover of his country. The state of trade must also tell very disastrously on agriculture, which for many years has been in a most depressed condition. The Bishop of Peterborough wrote a letter the other day, in which he said that he had a living in his gift which he could not dispose of, though its nominal value was £4BO a year, but at present is worth nothing, and what adds to the painful position of the clergy is that under the present depressed state of agricul- ture and trade the laity are unable to assist them. I wish, then, to ask whether the time has not come when we should seriossly ask ourselves whether some protection should not be afforded to the industry of the country. It is no ques- tion of class—all classes are equally affected; and no class will suffer more than that of the labourers, whose only ca- pital is the wages that they can earn by their labour. Is the country to be ruined for the sake of a theory ? I hope not, and that it will inquire into the causes of our present dis- tress and declare at the next general election, which cannot be far distant, that the present system of one-sided free Trade shall be abolished."

div.head: FEARFUL FIRE IN LONDON.
div.p: FEARFUL FIRE IN LONDON.
FIVE PERSONS KILLED.

A most disastrous fire broke out in one of the numerous small streets in Bishopsgate about 9-30 on Monday night, resulting in the death of five persons, injury to many more, and the destruction of a nine-roomed house. The fire was first discovered by a lodger, at No. 5, Windsor-street, a house let out to several tenants. Smoke was seen issuing from under the door of an apartment occupied by a newspaper seller named Fuller. The lodger, whose name was Barns, burst the door open, but was forced to retreat before the flames, which, rushing out, caught the staircase, and soon set the house in a blaze. The alarm of " fire" was at once raised, and hose cart and escape were quickly on the spot, the hydrants being set to work at once. It was estimated that though the house was of such limited capacity, about 50 persons were lodged therein, and the shrieks of the in- mates from the open windows was most distressing. Some were escaping from the windows at the risk of receiving severe injuries or being killed, and ethers managed to clamber along the roof to the adjoining houses. By 11 o'clock the fire was subdued, and as it was known that the bodies of several persons must be in the ruins, search was made. In the top front room were found the bodies of Patrick Galloway, aged 73, and Mary Ann Galloway, Lis wife. In the top back room, Mary Ann Murphy, aged 31. and her daughter Kate, aged six, and son Eugene, aged 13, were found—in all five persons. Some of those who were injured by jumping from the windows were taken to the Metropolitan Fiee Hospital and some to Guy's. John Frogley, aged 16, heroically assisted his mother to save six Younger children. It is not known how the fire broke out, and it is stated that the whole of the tenants were unin- sured.

div.head: TIIE EGYPTIAN QUESTION.
div.p: TIIE EGYPTIAN QUESTION.

LORD GRANVILLE'S NOTE TO THE POWERS. The Times epitomises as follows the circular note which Earl Granville has addressed to the Powers on the Egyptian question The subjects treated in the circular are divided into two classes those in which other countries are directly interested, and in dealing with which it is necessary to seek the concurrence of the European Powers; and those which more particularly concern the internal administration of Egypt, and are not regulated by international agreements. Taking first the questions in which Europe has a direct interest, the circular points out that recent occurrences have called special attention to the Suez Canal. The danger which threatened it during Arabi's initial period of success, its occupation by the ldritish forces in the name of the , Khedive and their use of it as a base of operations against the rebels, and, finally, the attitude assumed by the Canal Company and its servants at a critical moment of the campaign, constitute cogent reasons for seeking to regulate the international position of the waterway so as to avoid similar dangers and diffi- culties in future. The Government believes that the free and unimpeded navigation of the canal at all times, and its protection from damage or obstruction by warlike operations, are matters of general interest, and holds itself entitled to assume that its action in the late war, intended as it was to vindicate the authority of the lawful ruler of Fgypt, is admitted on all hands to have been consistent with the main- tenance of freedom and inviolability. In order to guard, however, against future misconceptions in whatever quarter, and to define with clearness the future position of the Canal, the Government suggests an agreement which might advantageously be come to between the Great Powers, and to which other nations would subsequently be invited to give their adhesion. . The proposed arrangement is that the Canal should be free for the passage of ships of every kind in all circumstances, but that pre- cautions should be taken against the abuse of this privilege by enacting that in time of war a limitation should be placed upon the time during which vessels of war belonging to a belligerent Power should be permitted to remain in the Canal, and that no troops or munitions of war should be disembarked, it is also proposed, for the further securing of the neutrality and freedom of the channel, that no hostilities shall be permitted in the Canal or its approaches or anywhere in the territorial waters of Egypt, even in the event of Turkey being one of the belligerents. The recurrence of an emergency resembling the late rebellion is provided for by a clause excepting measures necessary for the defence of Egypt from the operation of these restrictive enactments. It is further pro- vided by the suggested agreement that every Power shall be bound to bear the cost of the immediate repair of any damage which its vessels of war may chance to cause to the Canal; and that Egypt shall .take all measures within its power to enforce the conditions imposed upon the ships of belligerent Powers using the Canal in time of war. No fortifications are to be erected on the Canal or in its vicinity, and nothing in the agreement is to be construed as curtail- ing or afUcting the territorial rights of the Egyptian Government further than is expressly stipulated. With reference to the financial arrangements which ard placed by the Law of Liquidation under the protection of all the Powers, the circular states that the Government bslieves it possible to attain greater economy and simplicity in the management of the Daira estates and some other administration by changes which would in no way diminish the security of the creditors, and hopes shortly to be able to' lay before the Powers definite proposals for accomplishing this end. The taxation of foreigners in Egypt is another question which can be dealt with only by general consent, but Her Majesty's Government count with confidence upon the so-operation of the Powers in placing foreigners upon the same footing as natives with regard to taxation. The system of mixed tribunals established ty international agreement fpr the decision of civil suits between natives and foreigners was in January last prolonged fora year, and would naturally expire on the Ist day of February. The Government has naturally advised the Egyptian Ministry to propose a 'further prolongation of a, year, in the hope that during that period an amend- ment of the Egyptian code and procedure may be

effected. Of the cjiii.stions of the second class, which-refer to the internal brganisation of Egypt, and have never been the subjects of direct international agreement, the first and mod presedng is the organisation of a force for the main- tenance of publiesecurity against external or internal foes. On all grounds Her Majesty's Government think that the Egyptian army should be a small one, and that the duty of maintaining internal order should be entrusted, as far as practicable, to a separate force of gendarmerie and police. A strong desire has been expressed by the Khedive and his Ministers that British officers should be lent to,fill certain of the higher posts in the army Under the Command-in- Chief of the Khedive, and to this desire the Government are willing to accede for a time; and upon a system which would enable Egyptian officers to Attain to some of the higher commands. Instead of the Control, the Government recommend that the Khedive should appoint a single European financial adviser, without any authority to interfere in the direct administration -of the country. There is no subject ef more pressing importance to the natives of Egypt than the establishment of a system for the administration of justice among themselves and between them and the Government. This important question, coming home to every peasant in Egypt, is now taken up by the English Government, which trusts in a short time to ate effective measures pat in operation. Mr. Forster, and those who sympathise with his efforts to obtain the suppression of the slave trade and slavery in Egypt, will learn with pleasure that the circular declares it to be a - question which the Government have much at heart, and promises that no opportunity will be missed of ad7ising the Khedive to take such steps as are calculated to attain the end in view. Upon the great question of the development of political institu- tions in Egypt, the Government awaits'fartber reports from its representatives. It-is a question of great importance and complexity, requiring for its treatment very careful study of the circumstances of the country and people. Without pledging itself prematurely to any definite measures, the Government indicates, is might have been ancticipated, its desire to find the solution of the difficulty in the prudent , introduction of representative institutions, in some form L adapted to the present political intelligence of the people, ' and calculated to aid their future progress.

div.head: LIBERAL MEETING IN MID. CHESHIRE.
div.p: LIBERAL MEETING IN MID. CHESHIRE.

1 The annual meeting of the Sale and Ashton-on-Mersy branch of the Mid-Cheshire Liberal Association was held on Monday evening at the Sale Institute. Mr. George Rooke presided, and there were present Mr. W. Summers, M.P.. Mr. J. Fox-Turner, the Rev. J. Johnson, Mr. W. Milne, Mr, A. Nicholson, Mr. A. E. Paterson, Mr. F. Milne, Mr. F. J. Marlow, Mr. C. Chapman, Mr. J. Magson, Mr. B. L. Green, and other gentlemen. In opening the proceedings the CHAIRMAN said they were met that night to promote the well-being of their local asecre elation.. During the past year that association bad been fully maintained. They had now branches in every part of that wide constituency, and the Liberal Two Hundred could be at any time convened for the selection of candidates ta represent the party at the next election. Upon whom that chome would fall he could not sky, but in his opinion no better man could be found to fight their battle than Mr. G. W. Latham (applause), who was well acquainted with their needs and desires. If they could get some gentleman familiar with their circum- stances, and trained in a Free-trade school, to contest the division with Mr. Latham, and win as they intended to do— (applause)—then they would have in the House of Com- mons a representation of all classes and all interests in that constituency, instead of at present, and for years past, having only one class represented there, and that class the landlords. (Applause.) in conclusion, the Chairman said letters explanatory of absence had been received from Mr. G. W. LathamoMr. Hopkinson, Mr. V. K. Armitage, and Mr. T. Lloyd. He moved the first resolution, as follows : —"That this meeting of the electors and non-electors of the Sale polling district of Mid-Cheshire desires to express in the first place its unabated confidence in her Majesty's Go- vernment, and, vecondly, to offer its sincere and hearty congratulations to the Right lion. W. E. Gladstone upon the attainment of his fifty years of public service, and trusts that his life may be spared and streagth continued to en- able him for many years to come to act as the recognised head of the Government. (Cheers.)" Mr. J. FOX-TURNER seconded the resolution in an amus- ing speech. He said he had heard that Sale was "looking up," and that public attention was being directed to it. He always knew the people of Sale were politically a "peculiar people "—(laughter)---and there was much in the place to stimulate political studies. The climate was salubrious, tempered only with the genial odour of acres of cabbages-- (laugliter)—and any political student desiring to pursue in solitude his reading would find undisturbed conveniences for his purpose on Carrington Moss. (Laughter.) Sale by its geographical position was constituted the •advanced guard of Liberal epinion in Mid-Cheshire. It was from Sale that they commenced their march into the Tory wilderness and began to "cry aloud and spare not "—(laugh- ter and applause)—and it was from Sale he hopel that ultimately the cheering cry would proceed that the strong- hold of the Tories in Mid-Cheshire had been stormed, and that a flag of the right colour was waving from its bastions. (Applause.) Mr. SummEns, M.P., in supporting the resolution, criticised some recent utterances of Mr. P. E. Warburton, M.P., in regard to the accession of L;otel Derby to the Liberal Cabinet. It was hoped by the Conservatives at one time that Lord Derby would assume the leadership pf a "moderate party," composed of many moderate Liberals and numbers of Conservatives, but the hope of seeing Lord Derby in that position was now beyond the range of possi- bility. (Applause.) Another of their Conservative mem- bers, Mr. Wilbraham, Egerton, had been strongly objecting to the new rules of procedure, which he had said were designed to "take away absolute freedom of debate and of speech, and :place all power in the bands of the Prime Minister." (Laughter.) Instead of doing that, the rules left untouched all the rights and privileges of Parliament, and were intended to protect the House of Common, not against an invasion of its privileges of the Crown, bat against the loquacity of its own members. (Applause.) The object of the closure, in other words, was to enable Parlia- ment to legislate once more, and to do work as well as talk about doing it. (Applause.) When the Tory party came into power—if ever it did—it would see the advantage and usefulness of the new rules, and would put them into just and adequate operation. (Hear, hear.) The resolution was carried unanimously. Mr. Men Low moved a resolution expressing approval of the new rules of procedure, and contemplating with satis- faction the prospect of some progress in such measures of domestic reform as were urgently needed. Mt. F. MILNE seconded the resolution, which was sup- ported by Mr. B. L. GREEN, and adopted. The delegates to the Central Association were then elected, and the meeting closed with votes of thanks to the Chair- men and Mr. Summers for their services.

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

Over 5,000 persons have been affected by the failure in the South Wales tinplate trade, and great distress exists. A committee, of which Sir John Jones Jenkins, M.P., is chairman, has bem formed with the object of relieving the distress. GREAT FAILURE OF LIVERPOOL SIIIPOWNERS : LIABILI- TIES £3ooooo—At the London Bankruptcy Court, on Mon- day, the failure was announced of Messrs. Patrick George Carylll and George ALEenn, merchants and shipowners, of London, Liverpool, Ireland, Canada, and elsewhere, trading as Francis Carvil I and Son, the liabilities being returned at £30,000. Mr. Cooper, actuary, George-street, Mansion House, has been appointed receiver and manager of the estate.

BILLS or SALE AND FAILURES.—In the week e.nding January 13, 1883, there were 227 bills of sale in England and Wales, a decrease of 767 over those of the correspond- ing period last year • aed the failures gazetted numbered 213, an increase of three. The totals for portion of year to January 13, 1883, are bills of sale registered for Eng- land and Wales, 436, a decrease of 1,384 ; the failures gazetted number 399, an increase of seven.—Sfubts' Mer- cantile Gazette. THE LANCASHIRE IFON TRADE —There is still an absence of any push of business in the iron market. A few trans- actions of pig iron are reported since the quarterly meetings minimum rates, which in some cases makers are now in- clined to repeat, but generally buyers show no anxiety to give out orders, and the prices offered do not as a rule•come up to what makers are prepared to accept. Lancashire linkers of pig iron still ask 475. 6d., less 2i for delivery, equal to Manchestet ; a few offers have been made at a little under this figure, but have not as yet resulted in business. For district brands quotations remain at 475. to 48s. for Lincolnshire, and 48s. 6d. to 50s. for Derbyshire, less 23/4 delivered here, and makers as a rule are firm at these figures, but there are odd lots to be bought at 6d. or so less. There are very few ingairies for finished iron ; the nominal price remains at £6 10s., delivered into the Manchester district, but for specifications makers in most cases are willing to take £6 7s. 6d., and prompt orders could in some ifistauces be.placed as low as £6 Sc. THE LANCASHIRE COAL TRADE.—There has been no very material change in the condition of the coal trade of this district during the past week. Supplies of engine fuel in some cases are not very plentiful, owing to the limited quantity of round coal being screened, but generally there is scarcity of either bur.ey or slack. The pits, as a rule, are being kept fairly employed, but here and there a resort to short time has been found necessary. There is a good deal of low selling in the market, which renders it difficult for colliery proprietors to maintain their list rates, but it is only in exceptional cases that actual reductions are made in open quotations, and at the pit mouth the average prices .remain about as uder :-Best coal, 10s. to 105. 6d.; seconds. Bs. to Bs. 6d.; corrinon house coal, 6s. 61 to 75.; jams) and forge coal, 6s. to 6s. 6d.; burgy, 4s. 91. to 55.; and good slack, 3s. 6d. to 4s. per ton. The shipping trade is only quiet, and low prices as a rule have to be quoted to secure orders. For steam coal, delivered at Garston docks, it is difficult to get more than 7s. 9d. to Bs. per ton, and at the high level, Liverpool, there is plenty offering at as low as 7s. 6d. per ton. TEE CALEDONIAN RAILWAY STRIEE.—The Strike of railway employes on the Caledonian line is extending, and threatens to paralyse the Hamilton coal trade, which was rapidly reviving from extreme depression. Nearly every colliery for a distance of twelve miles has its sidings blocked with loaded waggons, and thousands of colliers on Wednesday were idle. Passenger traffic was more irre- gular on Wednesday, and trains were unusually late. The local engine sheds at Hamilton, in which 50 locomotives were stationed, havOeen closed, and the traffic is now con- ducted from Motherwell. The Edinburgh servants of the Caledonian Railway held a meeting on Wednesday, attended by about 200 persons, and resolved only to return to work upon orders from the secretary of the Railway Servants' Society. At Greenock passenger traffic on the Caledonian line was very much interrupted for over three hours. No trains could be despatched from or arrive at Greenock station. Three trains leaving Glasgow at different hours arrived almost simultaneously. Sufficient engines could not be run from Greenock.

MR. FORSTER ON COMMERCIAL LEGISLATION. Mr. Forster, speaking at a soiree of the Bradford Chamber of Commerce on Monday night, said that the Chambers of Commerce had done a great deal of good throughout the ' country. He was glad to think that efforts to obtain a - Minister of Agriculture and Commerce were at last likely to be successful. It was highly important that the offices should not be apart, for the two joined would give the Minister who held them more influence than if they were separate. He trusted that some alteration would be made whereby the Minister who was responsible to the House Of Commons for education should not alsq be responsible, as . was at present the case, for the ailments of cattle. Referring to forthcomin4 .legislation, he hoped that the Bankruptcy Bill which Mr. Chamberlain was to introduce would make an improvement in a state of law which was so bad at present. The new committees, it was expected, would be of much use in assisting the House of Commons in His ' labours, and would afford facilities for useful legislation On matters connected with agriculture and commerce. These interests, he contended, should not be considered -antago- nistic, but should be closely bound togetiler.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JANUARY 20, 1883.

Two very important despatches relating to Egyptian affairs have this week emanated from the Foreign Office, and the contents of these documents have been discussed more or less eagerly in all the capitals of Europe during the past few days. It has for some time been pretty well understood what the intentions of England were in the country which she has only recently conquered; but not until Tuesday were they fully disclosed, and we venture to think that no Government. calmly considering Lord GRANVILLE'S pro- posals, will hesitate to give them a cordial acquiesence It is scarcely to be expected, of course, that France would be satisfied From the first day of our intervention, single-handed in Egyptian affairs, France has been jealous of ourtactions, yet, When her present irritation passes away, we feel confident that even France will acknowledge we are adopting a generous, a conciliatory, and a wise policy. One of the'despatches has reference solely to the Joint Control, which, ever since the war, had been inoperative, and it ha-s now been definitely abandoned. In the past it may have been productive of some good, but it has always been a grievance to the Egyptians, and it would have been foolish to have attempted to revive it under the altered cir-. cumstances. Our Government accordingly accedes to the wish of the KHEDIVE and his Ministers that it shall be abolished, and its place they recommend should be filled by the KHEDIVE appointing a single European financial adviser, such appointment not to be dependent on the selection or consent of any foreign Government. The duties of this officer would be to attend Cabinet Councils (but not as a Finance Minister) when requested by the KHEDIVE, and to exercise, as His HIGHNESS might appoint, powers of inquiry and advice on financial questions, but without any authority to interfere in the direct administration of the country. He would, in fact, be in reality the accountant of the KHEDIVE, and his presence would be some security to the bondholders and a guarantee that no financial abuses would be tolerated. The Control went much further than this, for it enabled the Controllers to interfere in internal affairs, hence some of the complications which occasionally cropped up. The second despatch, which has been addressed to Her MAJESTY'S representatives at Paris, Berlin, Vienna, Rome, and St. Petersburg, is very much wider in its scope, and deals with the future administration of the country. The subjects treated are of two categories—those which concern other coun- tries and are matters for the consent or con- currence of the European Powers; and those which are matters of internal administration. In the former categoa, attention is naturally enough first called to the Suez Canal, and the Government submit an agreement for the sanction of the Powers to which the most hypercritical can scarcely take exception. Her MAJESTY'S Government say they believe that the free and unimpeded navigation of the Canal at all times, and its freedom from obstruction or damage by acts of war, are matters of importance to all nations; and to secure this in the future they propose that the Canal should be free for the passage of all ships in any'circumstances ; but to guard against the abuse of such a privilege it is provided that in time of war a limitation should be placed upon the time during which vessels of war belonging to a belligerent Power should be permitted to remain in the Canal, and that no troops or munition of war should be disembarked. It is also proposed, in order to guarantee the neutrality and free-

no hostilities shall dom of this waterway, that •• approaches or take place in the Canal or itb of Egypt, elsewhere in the territorial -wattA • b • -s ey eing and this even in the event of Tam, se one of the belligerents. Any rowelh any vessels of war happen to do P • damage to the Canal shall be :Donn to bear the ccst of it imn:L!diate repair ; and Egypt is to take all measures within its power to enforce the conditions imposed on the transit cl. belligerent vessels through the Canal in time of war. No fortifications are to .I,e erected on the Canal or in its vicinity; and further, nothing in the agteement is to be deemed to abridge or affect the territorial rights of the Government of Egypt further than is ex- pressly provided. Such, in brief, is the substance of the agreement relating to the Canal, the protection of which, as our high- way to -India, enforced us to interfere in Egyptian affairs; and to our mind the 'agree- ment does not contain any provision which will not operate to the advantage of all the great Powers in an equal degree. England at least is to have no special advantage, though, as the conquerer, she might fairly claim such. The other matters for inter- national arrangement relate to the taxation of foreigners equally with natives, and to a reform in the mixed tribunals for the trial of civil suits between natives and foreigners, about which there is not much difficulty, if any, likely to arise. With respect to the second class of questions, the Government point out that the most pressing of the measures of internal administration is the organisation of a force for the maintenance of public security against external or internal attack. 9n the grounds alike of economy and safety, the Government think the army should be small, and they propose that the duties should be discharged by a separate force of gendarmerie and of police. By desire of the KHEDIVE and his Ministers British officers will fill certain posts under the KHEDIVE'S Commander-in-Chief, but this is agreed to by England only on a system which will give Egyptian officers access to some of the higher commands. The scheme for the , reorganisation of the army is not yet com- pleted; but we may rest satisfied that it will be such a one as will not wound the suscepti- bilities of any foreign Power. In the new state of affairs it is just possible that England may derive advantages in Egypt, but certain it is English statesmen have no selfish end in view in the settlement of this difficulty; and if any advantages should accrue to our country, depend upon it it will be the result of accident only. Turkey has been afraid that we would assume a protectorate of the country ; but the SULTAN will be assured, on a study of the Note, that we are anxious to get out of it as soon as we can, though we cannot leave until the new organisa- tion is in thorough working order. France, on the other hand, charges 115 with breaking our engagements, and is annoyed at the abolition of the Joint Control. Seeing, however, that two of the three parties ihterested in that arrangement were desirous of being released from their obligations, we -should like to know what other course we could have adopted. A section of the French Press affects a somewhat haughty air at the tone of Lord GRANVILLE'S Note, and is using towards this country language which cannot be justified by the facts; but,France, we think, should be the last Power to offer any complaint, seeing how, at a critical moment, it left England in the lurch. Other Powers, we are glad to observe; view the Note in a very friendly light, and the more it is perused the more will it commend itself to the good judgment of every intelligent politician. The free navigation of the Suez Canal is by the agreement secured to all nations in time of peace ; an even in time of war all the Powers may use the water- way—as England did a short time ago— under certain limitations. The internal administration of Egypt is also placed upon what will doubtless prove a stable foundation; and we may fairly hope the country is on the road to give us no further cause for anxiety.

There is quite a gathering of distinguished English politicians on the shores of the Mediterranean. Lord Salisbury is at Cannes ; so is Mr. Gladstone. Sir Stafford Northcote is cruising on the blue waters, and Lord Randolph Churchill is in Algeria or " some- wl•ere on the other side." It is said to be highly probable that Sir Stafford Northcote will seek an interview with his chief at Caanes, and that Lord R indolph Churchill may drop in on his way home. The event would be historical if the four leaders of English political parties were to meet and exchange courtesies in that fashionable and expensive watering place. That there are a great many fools in this world is ahundantly proved by a case which came before the Birmingham magistrates one day this week. A gentlemanly -dressed man named Hartwell, who glories in a great many aliases, claims to be the "Great Seer of England," and who describes himself as " philo- sopher' astrologer, and grand master of mysteries," was charged with committing a series of advertising frauds, and the statements made in court show how easily people can be gulled. The " Seer " has on former occasions been convicted of exercising the mystic art; and in the present instance he was arrested through the instrumentality of a Yorkehire vicar, who sent to the Birmingham police copies of the prisoners advertisements in different papers offer- ing "news from the invisible world" for twenty stamps, talismans for victories over enemies from 103. to £5, celestial signs and characters on parchment or virgin gold, and further witching presents at equally reasonable terms. When apprehended the prisoner had upon him from 200 to 310 letters which he had recently received, and all of which had money en- closed. The letters, it need scarcely be said, are nearly all from girls and women; and in most cases the writers.sent the stamps for what is called their "seven years' future." In some cases mothers wrote asking the future of their children. I sincerely hope Hartwell will be severely punished for so imposing upon the credulity of simple people, yet I think if some of the persons thus imposed upon could be punished we should hear a great deal less of this cla e e! imposters. The Duke of Rutland has this week revived a very ' old cry, no less important a one than that of "Protec- tion," but I fear his Grace will experience a difficulty in finding people to answer to it. In a letter which he has published, the Duke asks whether in the opinion of the greater number of Englishmen the time has not arrived when some endeavour should be made to save England, before it be too late, from her down- ward commercial course. Competition, he says, has increased, and is increasing, in every branch of busi- ness, and the margin of profit is cut so close in conse- quence that there is a distinct diminution in the stay- ing power of traders. The Duke, therefore, inquires whether the time has not come when we should seri- ously ask ourselves whether some protection should not be afforded to the industry of the country. Is the country, he asks, to be ruined for the sake of a theory? He hopes not, and that it will inquire into the causes of our present distress, and declare at the next general election, which, we are told, cannot be far distant,- that the present system of one-sided free trade should be abolished. The country, I venture to think, will do no such thing; the electors, and the working -class portion of them more especially, have experienced too much of the benefits of free trade ever to trample the principle under foot. His Grace mast really be living in a state bordering on "Egyptian darkness," and the sooner the Cobden Club takes the Duke in hand and enlightens him the better it will be for him and for those whom he presumes to instruct.

The Caledonian Railway servants are now on strike, and to me it is a matter of surprise that the crisis has been so long delayed. They demand that their working hours shall be reduced, and that it is necessary they should be shortened no one acquainted with what they have to endure can deny. An in- fluential Scotch journal remarks that the point brought into prominence in the strike is not whether the working week of the men "should be one of fifty-four or one of fifty-seven hours, such as has roused other trades to action in bygone days; but it is whether they should require to hang on at im- portant duty till nature is so exhausted that they fall asleep clutching the handles of the critical levers on the accurate moving of which the lives of hundreds of travellers depend." We are told that at one of the meetings of the men an engine driver stated that in one week he worked 96 hours, his spell of duty on ' the Thursday lasting 23i hours! A pointsman put in 200 hours' duty in a single fortnight. A goods guard for twenty consecutive days had 360 working hours, or an average of eighteen hours a day. At one important and intricate junction a driver fell asleep while watching for a signal to proceed. Another fell asleep in passing an important branch, and in his dazed state when he awoke stopped his train, believing he was travelling the wrong road. Another worn-out man did, in his sleep, let his engine off upon the wrong line of rails, and was in- debted for his safety to the prompt action of his fire- man. These statements never having been contra- dicted, we are entitled to assume they are substantially correct. And do they not, may I ask, throw a flood of light on the dangers of railway travelling, especially on the Caledonian line ? The men, if they are firm, are bound to succeed; and they are deserving the thanks of the public for coming out, if for no other reason than that they direct the powers that be to a state of affairs which Mr. Chamberlain, the President of the Boara of Trade, will no doubt remedy. TIIE DREADFUL WOUNDING CASE AT WIDNES. - There is every evidence that the offence with which Wm. Percy is charged will assume a more serious aspect. A fortnight has elapsed since Mrs. Percy was found in the kitchen of her husband's farm at Moss Bank, covered with blood, and in a state of insensibility. She has never regained complete consciousness, and notwithstanding the skill of the medical men she continues to become worse each day. Her nourish- ment consists of port wine and similar stimulants, and on several occasions a ray of consciousness has seemed to visit her, and she has muttered feebly. She is now very weak, and very little hope of her recovery is held out. Consider- ing the poor woman's age, the wonder is that she should have existed so lon,. Her husband, who is 72 years of age, veils any remorse be may feel at the deed he is charged with committing, under a stolid and indifferent demeanour, and on Monday, and again on Wednesday, when be was brought up at the Police Court for remand, he did not at all seem I affected by the proceedings. He will be kought before the I magistrates this morning, when probably he will again be remanded. Immediately his suffering victim regains her senses, should such an occurrence take place, her depositions will be taken.

Although so young, her career had been a very sad one. div.head: LOCAL AND GENERAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL AND GENERAL NOTES.

The memorial presented by the Ratepayers' Asso- ciation to the members of Widnes Local Board at their last meeting, asking them to consider the ad- visability of dividing the town into wards, gave rise to an interesting discussion, which had, however, no practical result. The advantages claimed for the scheme propounded by the deputation were not very apparent nor very numerous. To say that because certain towns have adopted a certain method of local government it must, perforce, be a beneficial one, is a corollary which few persons will be inclined to accept. Widnes has a market, which is a heavy incubus on the rates; does it, therefore, appear to the ratepayers of Bacup, who do not know this fact, that a market is a beneficial institution ? Measures, in all instances, must be adapted to circumstances. The division of Warrington into wards gives pre- dominence to a party, which could not maintain it if a poll of the town as a whole was taken. Liverpool is crying out under a somewhat similar grievance. I do not assert that the division made by the memo- rialists is not just, but I mention these instances to show that the change they crave is not the unmixed blessing they would have the ratepayers believe. Doubtless it has its advantages under certain condi- tions, but cheapness is hardly one. Printing is pro- bably one of the heaviest items in the bill of costs at election time. Will this be lessened? Aesuredly not, for instead of one set of voting papers sufficing for the whole town, five different and separate lots would be required. The cost of the latter would be much greater than the former. There would be for each ward a presiding officer with his staff who would have to receive the voting papers and convey them to some central place. This is the reverse of simplification, which Mr. T. Sadler con- tended would ensue. Mr. T. Sadler also claimed another advantage for the system he advocated on behalf of the memorialists : that each ward repre- sentative would see that borrowed money was ex- pended on the object for which it was obtained, the implied accusation being quickly discerned by Mr. F. H. Goseage, the ehairmaia, and repudiated by the speaker. There are two contending forces on the Board at present. Apparently, although we are told unity is strength, Mr. Sadler wishes to see five. He anticipates good results through each ward represen- tative, like the chieftain of a clan, fighting for his own. In towns, however, where elections take place in wards, the members of the governing body do not devote themselves to the interests of one locality. They govern for the good of the town as a whole, and if the members of Widnes Local Board do not spend the town's money in a proper manner under the present constitution, they would not if elected by wards. In fact, under the present loose system of voting, the division sought after would serve no good end. The Ratepayers' Association would confer a much greater boon upon the public if they would obtain voting by ballot, which could be done by a little persistent agitation. Then, as a matter of con- venience, and for no other reason, the town would probably be partitioned. Elections for members of the Local Board, as now conducted, are liable to so much abuse that any alteration in the method would be hailed with satisfaction, and for the Ratepayers' Association to be the means of substituting the ballot, would be a feat worth recording in their annals, and is one they ought to strive to accomplish. POACHING NEAR WIDNES.—James Whittle, Thos. Ryan Carr, and James Corrigan were summoned before the Widnes Bench, on Wednesday, on a charge of having trespassed on land over which Mr. Anderson, of Liverpool, has the right of shooting, in pursuit of game.—Whittle pleaded not guilty, Corrigan said he was not guilty, and Carr did not put in an appearance.—Mr. S. Marsh, of St. Helens, prosecuted.—lt was stated by Henry Paine, gamekeeper to Mr. Anderson, that on the 16th December he and another man, who ac- companied him, saw four men on the land in question, at Ditton. They were apparently digging out a rabbit, but on seeing witness and his companion they ran away. Witness and his companion gave chase, and caught the three defen- dants in a farmyard, the fourth man, whom they did not identify, escaping.—The Bench, considering the charges to be proved, fined each defendant lOs and costs.

A HARD CASE AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Patrick Highland was brought up on remand, charged with stealing a quantity of coal, warth Id., the property of Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co. It appeared that P.S. Clarkson met the prisoner making his exit from Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon's yard at half past seven on Satur- day morning, with the coal in his possession. He detained the prisoner, who, in answer to his inquiries, said he had no fire at home, and he was taking the coal to make one. He offered to restore it to the place where he had taken it from. —Mr. Joseph Morrison (manager) said the firm did no wish to press the charge against the prisoner, who was for- merly in a good position, but meeting with an accident, he was for some time in the hospital, and since then his mind appeared to be affected. Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon and Co. gave the prisoner employment in charity, as they felt some sympathy with him on account of the position he had formerly occupied. Mr. Brock: He is treating you rather badly.—The prisoner admitting stealing the coal, and Mr. Brock (the chairman) said although it was usual in these cases to send the prisoners to gaol without the option of a fine, the Bench, in consideration of the cir- cumstances, would in this instance impose a fine of 215., or in default, 14 days' imprisonment.—The prisoner had no money, and was taken to gaol.—The magistrates in the case were Mr. John Brock and Mr. F. H. Gossage. CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT PRESTON BROOK. At the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before the Rev. E. A. P. Campbell and Mr. Charles Reynolds, William Craddock, a young man, was charged with having, on the 6th December, at Preston Brook, unlawfully and cruelly ill-treated a mare by working the same in an unfit state.—Mr. 0. Harper; inspector to the R.S.P.C.A., said about one o'clock on the day in question he was on the canal bank at Preston Brook. He noticed the defendant in charge of a chesnat pony, which was attached to a cart which he was loading with rubbish. He went to him and found that the pony was very old, extremely thin, lame in all its legs, and in a most weak condition. The animal had a wound the size of a crownpiece on its fetlocks; a wound of the same size on its back, and another upon the off shoulder. All the wounds were extremely painful, and the horse was totally unfit to work. The wound upon the back had been covered with grease from the cart wheel, thus showing that some person was aware of the state of the horse.—The defendant pleaded that he was ignorant of the state of the horse, which he had only borrowed for a day.—lt appeared that the deendant had been twice con- victed of a similar offence, and the Bench fined him £l. and costs 10s. 6d., or a month's imprisonment. TILE FATAL ACCIDENT AT 'WIDNES DOCK. —MT. T. W. Barker, the coroner, held an inquiry at the Mersey Hotel, Widnes, on Saturday morning, touching the death of Thos. Tomkinson, an old man 72 years of age, who was killed by a locomotive engine while crossing a siding near the London and North-Western Dock. The deceased was a waterman on board the fiat Jessie, and was a native of Northwich. Mr. Ferrand, of Liverpool, represented the railway com- pany. From the evidence of Eliz tbeth Hulse, the daughter of the deceased; John Atherton, captain of the Jessie; Geo. Mort, the engine driver; and Win. Collier, the fire man, it appeared the deceased left the-flat, which was lying at the dock side, about twenty minutes to nine on Friday morn- ing, for the purpose of fetching a loaf; but instead of travelling along the quay side, he walked across the metals, which was a common practice, although legally not allowed. An engine which was travelling along the siding knocked him down, and passed over him, inflicting injuries from which he died in a few !Minutes. -It appeared that the engine was not travelling faster than "walking speed" when the deceased was knocked down. Mr. Ferrand, in. reply to the Coroner, said the sidings by the dock were the railway company's property, and the arrangements had been sanctioned by the Board of Trade.—The Coroner said the place seemed to be a very dangerous one, but as long as it was sanctioned by the Board of Trade, they could not inter- fere.—A verdict of accidental death was returned, coupled with a recommendation to the effect that new notice boards should be put up in the locality where the accident hap- pened, warning the public of the dangers they were in from engines and wagons. A WIDNES JURY AND TIIE CORONER. —At the con- clusion of an inquest held by Mr. T. %V. Barker, the coro- ner, at Mersey Hotel, Widnes, on Saturday morning, the foreman (Mr. Barnett Dutton) said before they separated he desired on behalf of the jury to congratulate Mr. Barker on his accession to the post of coroner. (Hear, hear.) He had served under coroners for 2-5 years, and he could testify to the courtesy and kind-heartedness which Mr. Barker had always displayed towards everybody in the fulfilment of the duties of his office, which they hoped he might long lire to occupy.—The Coroner replied that he was extremely grati- fied at their expression of good will. He had served a rather long apprenticeship of seven years before succeeding to the post, and in the course of that period he had unfortunately been called upon to visit Widnes very often. When he said unfortunately, he did not mean personally, but alluded to the lamentable occurrences which had brought him thither; for while the foreman had kindly said that he had always treated them kindly, he must testify that he had always received the greatest courtesy himself from Widnes juries. It had been a source of. great satisfaction to him to have been received so kindly by every jury he had met in the neighbourhood. Wherever he had gone, he had been greeted with very courteous expressions, and if anything could compensate him for the hard work of his office—for it was hard work to bold, as he often did, two or three in- quests a day, and to travel about so much—it would be such tokens of regard as these. He hoped he might have the pleasure of meeting them many many times, not in the re- lation of coroner and jurydan, but personally and privately. It always gave him great pleasure to meet afterwards anyone who had been on one of his juries, and he hoped he would frequently see them in time to come. (Applause.) —The proceedings then terminated.

PRIMITIVE METHODISM AT WIDNES: SALE OF WORK.—A sale of work, having for its object the reduction of the debt of £BOO which exists upon Simm's Cross Primitive Metho- dist Chapel, was held in that place of worship on Wednes- day afternoon. The " sale" had been organised by a ladies' committee, who, with the aid of Messrs. Draught, Rollason, Wiles, and Price, had also carried out the decorations, which had a pleasing effect. The goods offered for sale were of the usual miscellaneous description. No. 1 stall was in charge of Mrs. Rollason and Mrs. Lee; No. 2 (toys), Miss F. Wiles, Miss Barker, and Miss Shaw ; No. 3 (*dra- pery), Mrs. Bedggood, Mrs. Munslow, and Mrs. Wiles. The refreshment stall was under the superintendence of Mrs. Hughes, Mrs. Adams, and Mrs. Butler. There was a moderate attendance of the public at the opening ceremony, which was performed by the Rev.'l. Morton, superintendent minister, Warrington. In doing so the rev, gentleman ob- served that the object which had brought them together was a very high and noble one. It was to endeavour to wipe off the debt of £BOO which existed on their building. A debt of this kind, however, was not always to be neces- sarily regarded as a calamity. He believed it was some times a healthful thing; for it prevented their energies flag- ging, as they were apt to do when they had no difficulties to contend with. There was no danger, he thought, of the Primitive Methodists of Simm's Cross falling into this danger, because even when the debt was wiped off their original project would yet have to be fulfilled, and the task would need all their zeal and energy to bring it to a suc- cessful consummation. kApplause.)—The sales were then briskly proceeded with. During the afternoon and evening several musical performances were given by the choir and friends, and were a successful feature in the affair. On Thursday evening a tea party was held, followed by an entertainment of sacred music, in which Messrs. J. R. Lea and F. C. Davies. of Farnworth, assisted. Tile Rev. J. ACCIDENT AT WIDNES FOUNDRy A MAN SERIOUSL)I INJURBD.—At Widnes Foundry, on Tednesday, Thomas Nain, a labourer, 28 years ef age, and living at 25, H son-street, received injuries which necessitated; :he amputa- tion of his left leg at the knee. He is being atteNed at Widnes Accident Hospital by Dr. McLennan, and was yesterday in!a fair way towards recovery . He received his injuries whilst helping a eang of men to lift an iron casting of saveral tons weight, when the ponderous weight slipped from the chain, and struck Nain, dislocating his shoulder, , .4nd completely smashing his left leg. The other men for- tunately contrived to escape to a. safe distance. A HEARTLESS I.4ATITER AT WIDNES. —At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, a man named I'Valter Bushell was charged with neglecting to support his wife and family, in consequence of which they had become chargeable to the Prescot Union.—Mr. Scannel, relieving officer, stated that on the 3rd January he had found defendant's wife and two children in a lodging-house, in James-street, in a destitute condition. Defendant's wife and children had on two previ- ous occasions become chargeable to the Union, and the total sum owing by him to the Guardians was £4 23.—Defendant was sent to gaol for 14 days' hard labour.

RUNCORN Sots oF TEMPERANCE. On Monday, the Grand Division of the Order of Sons of Temperance held their annual session in the Grange-lane schoolroom, Birken- head, the opening. ceremony being perferrned by Brother J. Hitchen, G.W.P., of Crewe. Representatives weie present from Runcorn and other districts in Cheshire. The Grand Scribe (Mr. T. Cooke, of Runcorn) stated, in his report, that there had been an increase in the funds of £BO, and an increase of 70. members. Mr. Thomas Faulkser (Runcorn) was appointed G.W.P.rand Mr. Coohe war re-elected Grand Scribe, which post he has filled for six years. Mr. John Jones was re-appointed Grand Treasurer; and Mr. John Halford (of Weston) and Mr. Cook (of Handley) were ap- pointed auditors. Mr. Cooke, the Grand Scribe, was ap- pointed a representative to the National Grand Lodge Meeting, to be held at Barrow-in-Fumes, in Whit-week. We may state that only one death has been reported during the half-year ; and that the meetieg "centralised " the funds of the cadet section.

At the Quarter Sossions for the county of Lancaster held in the Crown Court, St. George's Hall, Liverpool,this week, the following prisoners from Widnes were tried with the results undermentioned:—John Power (18), labourer, charged with having at Widnes, on the 28th ult., stolen 44 lbs. of scrap iron, the property of the Widnes Metal Com- pany, was sentenced to twelve months' imprisonment.— Stephen Scally (20), labourer. charged with having on the 27th ult., at Widnes, damaged a window in the shop of Mr. Syred, pawnbroker, to the extent of £5 103.9 was found net guilty and discharged.—Thomas Smith (17), was sentenced to six months' imprisonment and three years' police super- vision, for stealing a quantity of lrad, the property of James Muspratt and others, at Widnes.—Catherine Matthew (28), and Henry Stowles (25) were charged with stealing a pair of clogs, the property of William Shea, at Widnes on the 4th of November, and, being found guilty, the female prisoner was sentenced to nine month, and the male prisoner to three months' imprisonment. PRESENTATION AT ItuNconx.—On Thursday evening the choir of the Newtown Mission Church and a few friends met at the National School for the purpose of making a presentation to Mr. John Pownall, who is about to leave the town, having accepted a similar situation to the one he held at the Parish Church Schools—that of assistant master— in Sunderland. The Rev. R. Edwards presided. He re- marked upon Mr. Pownall's long connection with the mission, to which he had given such valu- able help since it started, and expressed his re- gret at his departure. In the absence of Mr, Moores, Mr. R. Wainwright made the presentation, acccmpanied with a few appropriate remarks. The present consisted of a handsome writing desk and 10 volumes, which included Macauley's and Sydney Smith's essays, and the poetical works of Hemans Cooper, Moore, and Hoed. The books contained the following inscription : "Presented 'o Mr. John Pewnall by the choir and friends of the Newtown Mission Church in token of their esteem, and as a slight acknowledgement of the valuaole services rendered for the past 15 years. Runcorn, January 18th, 1883."

MARRIAGE OF MR. R. M. BROOKE. On Tuesday, the marriage of Mr. Richard Marcus Brooke, eldest son of Sir Richard Brooke, of Norton Priory, of Walton, with Miss Crawley, eldest daughter of Mr. J. S. Crawley, Stockwood Park, Bedfordshire, was celebrated in the Parish Church, Luton. Owing to the bride's father living in the immediate neighbourhood, the event excited a large amount of local interest, and the large church was well filled with specta- tors. Mr. Lionel Brooke act Was best man, and the five bridesmaids wen the Misses Mabel, Winifred, and Lily Brooke, and the Misses Crawley. The officiating clergy- men were the Rev. H. M. Wells? of Priestwood rectory, Great Missenden, Bucks, and the Rev. A. ,Buchanan, of Kingswalden rectory. Although the weather in the early part of the meeting was of an unpromising kind, before the ceremony had been concluded the sun shone in a most auspicious manner. A large number of guests attended the wedding breakfast, and the presents which were very numerous and costly, were much admired. After the break- fast the bride and bridegroom left for the Isle of Wight.' On Saturday evening last the bridegroom was presented at Norton Priory with a beautiful illuminated address by Mr. Bennett, Mr. J. W. Baguley, and Mr. D. T. Baguley, on behalf of the tenants. On the same evening a second deputation, consisting of the vicar, Mr. Baguley (churchwarden) and Mr. Peacock (organist) waited on Mr. Brook and presented him with, on behalf of the congregation, a handsome Bible, prayer book, and hymn book, each containing a suitable in- scription. Besides numerous other presents the labourers on the estate presented Mr. Brooke with a pair of handsome crystal larnps,°and the servants of the household presented him with a silver kettle.
