At a recent meeting of the provisional committee of the Manchester Ship Canal scheme, it was reported that the Parliamentary deposit had been made. The subscrip- tions to the guarantee fund of £lOO,OOO were reported to have reached the silm of £155,000, and the call of 20 per cent, to be in course of payment.

MLNCIIESTEB, ASSIZES.--These Assizes will be opened to-day (Saturday), the 20th inst. The court will sit on Monday at eleven am., and on every other day during the assizes at ten a.m., unless otherwise directed. There are 33 prisoners for trial, two of whom are charged with murder, seven with manslaughter, nine with burglary, three with robbery, three with bigamy, two with libel, and the remainder with stealing a post letter, concealment of birth, forgery, assaults, and arson.

PROPOSED NEW Lib/CAM:IRE RAILWAY.—The pro- posal to throw a high-level bridge over the estuary of the Ribble has, in view of the bill for the development of the Ribble at an estimated cost of about half a million, been abandoned. The new bridge was part of the new scheme to connect the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire, Great Northern, and Midland Railways directly with Blackpool. The new arrangements are for the Cheshire Lines to be extended from Wigan to Longton on the West Lancashire Railway, seven miles from Preston. The new line will be formed down the coast from Blackpool to Preston, joining the West Lancashire. There will be two stations at Blackpool, where the line will run underground from the south to the north end. The new railway will put Blackpool in direct communication with all parts of the country. LATEST NEWS.
. ROYALIST CONSPIRACY IN FRANCE.

FRENCH OFFICERS IMPLICATED. A Paris telegram says :—Prince Napoleon still remains at the Conciergerie. Some of the morning papers speak of the discovery of a Legitiruist conspiracy, assuming the title of the Catholic Alliance, and forming a vast associa- tion, directed by M. de Charette. Its objects are alleged to be the overthrow of the Republic even by force of arms. It is added that 33 legions have been formed in the West and Centre, that several officers of the Army are implicated, anal that de:Zts of arms eNist.

THE MYSTERIOUS DISCbVERY IN LONDON. The Press Association's West Ham correspondent says : Th e story that the body of a girl found in a box at Clerken- well is that of one of those who disappeared from West Ham. is discredited there, but it causes a deep impression, and the local police authorities went yesterday to London to inquire. into the matter.

div.head: LOST HEIRESS.
div.p: THE LOST HEIRESS.

A Dublin correspondent says :—T-he story of the missing heirese has gained fresh interest by the fact that a letter has- been received from a Mary Anne Shaw, of Bristol, saying that she had been left on a doorstep in Kingstown when she was scarcely a month old, and lived in Kingstown till she was thirteen years of age. She requests that the par- ticulars reported to the police at the time the child was found on Mr. Carey's steps should be at once forwarded to her, as she- is strangely inclined to believe that she is the missing heiress.

TERRIBLE EXPLOSION IN HOLLAND: FORTY PERSO2.7S KILLED. An Amsterdam telegram of yesterday says :—Three terrific eXplozions occurred this morning at the gunpowder manufactory situated near Minden, three leagues distant from this city. The shock was so great as to unroof nearly all the houses in the town of Minden. Much damage has also been done in the neighbouring towns and villages. The loss of life is not yet known, but it is feared that not less than forty persons have perished. The explosions were beard here and in the Eastern suburb of the city. The window panes in several houses were trJken. IRISH ANARCHY. SAVAGE ATTACK ON THE VICEROY. The following placard is being widely circulated in Ire- land, printed in thick, black type, on lavender-coloured paper :—" Remember Francis D. Hynes, done to death by twelve drunken Castle hacks. Remember Patrick Walsh, the evicted widow's son. Remember Myles Joyce, mangled and tortured in his death agony because he dared to assert his innocence on the scaffold. Remember all the victims to bribed judges, of packed juries, of salaried and perjured witnesses, some rotting in British convict prisons, and others happier in that they have gone beyond the reach of landlord spite and the revengeful cruelty of Dublin Castle. Remember the little children of the poor labouring man, who gasped out their harmless lives in the anguish of fever, denied the shelter of a roof or the comfort of a fire by the demon in human form whcr reigns in the soft luxuriance of the Viceregal Lodge, paid for by the people whom he op- presses for a pastime, and over whose sufferings he gloats. Remember the massacre of Ballina by order of the English Herod—the childless earl who wreaks the envy of Lis joy- less old age on the humble homes and hearts of the Irish peasantry. Show that you remember these things, and re- ceive Spencer with a welcome according to his works."

STOCK AND SHARE MARKET. Messrs. Joseph R. and W. P. Baines, share brokers. 13, Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchezter, write kJan. 18tb): A fair amount of business has been concluded during the past • week, and, looked at as a whole, the tone of the market is pretty steady. Railway earnings have not given much strength to that market, and as a consequence lower prices have ruled in many of the leading stocks, but the depreciation in values is not severe, and the feeling now more hopeful than has been the case during a portion of the week. What business is reported in the several descriptions of miscellaneous shares is of a general character, no one class showing any marked stir. Prices a.ised compa-e favourably with those lately obtained, there being very few instances in which special remark is called for.

And this, let it be remembered, not by any choice of - an individual, Or wish of a family, but as an expression of the thought of the teachers of the day, who in this matter do but too accurately interpret the thought of the people whom they lead! I am given to und'erstand that a very large, if not the largest, proportion of funerals in Paris are of this same description. The element of religion is excluded. Now it seems to me that all this may be fairly pointed to as illustrating the failure of a State religion to make a nation religious, and as showing how a State religion may even- tually lead to a :icicle revolt against religion of every kind. Ills profoundly -significant, 1 think, that a man of Gam- betta's calibre' whose force of character no one can question, was compelled to suppress whatever regard for religion he possessed. If incidents in his later years are correctly reported, there are not wanting tokens that he still main- tained an affection for the faith in which he had been trained as a youth. Among these is one connected with no little beauty and naturalness with the memory of his mother. It is said that it was ever a cus- tom with him to have tapers burnt in the parish church near his residence on each anni- versary of his mother's death. On the last anniversary but one, lie was passing the church door arm in arm with a Republican senator, when he suddenly stopped, and said "I always burn a taper on this day. I had forgotten all about it." Saying this, he moved towards 1 the door; but his friend remonstrated with a smile," What will the clericals say if they heard it ?" " Bah !" answered he "they shall say I always loved my mother !" He walked into the church, ordered the tapers, and, as the vicar of the church testifies in the Times this week, bowed his , knees for some moments in the posture of prayer before the altar. Thus would Gambetta seem to have retained, until at any rate a recent date, a respect for religious observances, and surely some faith in religion itself. The striking point is that he had to make it so secret. The whole thing shows that a nation is not made religious by any State arrange- ment, and that if the State religion be left to itself, sooner or later it will do the very thing it is meant not to do, and make the nation revolt against the idea and the observance of religion altogether. I forbear to follow this matter any further, but with so striking an illustration of my point freshly before our minds, I could not pass it by without reference. None of these things upon which I have been dwelling can made a nation religious. No occasional acknow- ledgments, no keeping Sundays from secular uses, no State establishment of religion. Nothing can make a nation religions except making it individually religious. Now, my friends, let us deal candidly with the grave subject to-night. We all believe in the value of religion; we all wish our nation to be religious. Let us ask the question honestly: Is the majority of our nation possessed by the religious spirit? We have had this question put in front of us a good deal in recent times-by the statistics collected about church and chapel attendance, by the statements of men who work in Christ's name among the vast masses of the working classes, and of the lowest and poorest and worst of our population. lam not goint to repeat what has been said over and over again in respect of the diminished attendance on public worship, except to say this, that it is impossible to avoid the conviction that recent statistics have in the main been accurate. Now that may not mean of necessity a diminished regard for religion in this country. It may simply mean, and I think it does very largely mean, that they who went to church for custom and form's sake, stay away now that it has become equally respectable to stay away. Therefore, there may be as much real regard for religion in-the land now as ever; perhaps even more. But it is also true that numbers of these abstainers from worship have no care for religion. Add then these hosts of " respectable " non-church goers to the hosts of the openly irreligious, profane, dissolute, criminal, even heathen classes, and you have a fearful multi- tude of the population either indifferent to, or ignorant of, or , hostile to, religion. It remains a fact, that our legal observance of Sundays, our establishment of religion, our free churches, our mis- sions, our revivals, our open air preaching, our house to house visitations, our Sunday Qchools, our tracts, our Bibles, have not yet brought to the feet of Christ what we fear is the majority of the inhabitants of this realm. I very much doubt if we at all adequately know the real religious condi- tion of our nation. It strikes me as probable that there is vastly more ignorance of religion, and absolute hostility to religion, than we are accustomed to imagine. It may pro- bably appear very incredible, for example, that in this so- called Christian England, with its houses of worship prominent in every throughfare, and their steeples pointing with silent finger to heaven from the midst of every ham- let., with its Bibles, prayer-books, tracts, Sunday schools, missions, that there could be found any who have reached the adult age ignorant as to who Jesus Christ is, and why He came into the world. Yet such there are! A brother minister in this country, pastor of a church aided every year by a grant from the society I plead for tofilay, told me only last Wednesday this striking and startling fact. Hay- ing entrusted to him some money to distribute among the very poor, he entered a house where he knew there was need. Resolving, if possible, to give the woman whom be found there not only the" bread which perisheth," but also some knowledge of the "Bread of Life," he questioned her as to what she knew about religion. Astonished at the ignorance displayed in her answers, he at length plainly asked whether she knew who ' he heard her reply that she had never heard of Jesus Christ was. And to his amazement azeThenatt she knew nothing about Him, that she had no idea about , religion, and had never thought of praying. This woman ! was a collier, and bad passed her life in a colliery district, is living at this moment in this country, not 20 miles away. ' Nor may we suppose her case by any means a solitary in- stance, Any large towns have whole streets in them from which no individual man, woman, Child even find their way to church or school. They are born, they live, they die in ignorance of Christ and His truth. This ignorance of religion is far greater than we dream of in this land of Sabbaths, Bibles, and Churches and Christianity! Nor is our country free from ho.tility to religion. Mr. Charles Bradlaugh, and men who think with him, have a large fol- lowing. How large it is difficult to say; but the signs are

greater measure than that entailed by their personal loss. (Hear, hear.) But still we live, and, taken all in all, I think we thrive. Let me now give yon some figures which I think are interesting. We began 1877 with 17] upon the roll of church membership. Since January, 1877, it has been my pleasure to welcome into church fellowship 176 persons, 51 by transfer from other churches, and 125:upon profession of faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. During the six years our church roll has suffered the loss of 114 members-16 by death, 35 by transfer to other churches, fallen out of membershin„ chiefly and 63 have, or on ledgoa 5e anothei I by non-attendance or removo 4- .. .. °Leer localities without seeking toe usual trans- fer. Of the original 171 upon the '..:1.1 on January 15t,1877, only 100 still remain with us ; a somewhat striking token of the life of change which we live. And yet, instead of the 171 with which we bega;-k 1877, we began 1883 with 248. (Applause.) Among other items of interest, note- worthy in six years' history, is that I baptized no less than 150 babies—(laughter)—a hopeful sign, assuring us that if only the children tread in the footsteps of their parents, Wycliffe will not want for a congregation in the time to come. As a people, we are slow at getting married— (laughter)—but I have been honoured by tying the knot for 40 couples, since six years ago. Turning now to matters of finance. I have collected the following facts. During the six years of which I am speaking the following sums have been raised and expended by the constituents of Wycliffe Church, congregation, and schools :—The weekly offering for expenses of public worship, £4,035 3s lid; Sunday school work, £541 Os 4,j-d; home missions, including Cockhedge Mission and Lancashire Congregational Union, £935 4s 21; foreign missions, London Missionary Society, church and school, £739 is 7d; other objects: Hospitals, Lancashire College, chapel building society, &,c., £1,409 15s BRl—total, £7,660 5s 10d. Besides this, in con- nection with the day school, the sum of £4,656 3s 7d has been received during this period • thus making the Wycliffe turn-over amount to no legs than £12,316 9s 5d in six years. (Applause.) I venture to think these facts and figures are interesting. And while we have every need to rally well together, and enlist every hand in some work of usefulness, we have no need to be downhearted. Our past is a matter for thankfulness. Our future should excite our hope and call forth our trust. We are united in the best of causes, and if faithful to our duty we shall win the truest of rewards. (Applause.) The excellent programme of vocal and instrumental music was then proceeded with. Want of space, however, precludes us from referring particularly to any of the items, all of which, judging by the applause bestowed, seemed to give much pleasure to the audience. Still special mention must be made of the able recitations by W. Rigby, Esq., who Ikept the assembly in a continual roar of laughter. The programme was as follows : Overture " Z ‘rnpa" and T. R. Ford

div.head: WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH. ANNUAL TEA MEETING.
div.p: WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH. ANNUAL TEA MEETING.

About 250 persons attended the annual tea party in con- nection with Wycliffe Congregational Church, held in Wycliffe Hall, on Thursday evening. The hall was taste- fully and effectively decorated with numerous texts and mottoes, conspicuous amongst which was the church motto for 188," Walk humbly with thy God," placed at the top end of the room immediattlY behind the platform, The latter was also neatly ornamented. and ':o.e table was the word " Winne," formed in large characters of white WCiol on a crimson ground. The decorations made the ball look very bright and attractive, and were the work of Miss Mackenz.i.q., nho deserves praise for the able manner in which she had tarried out the embellishments. After tea there was a public meeting and entertainment, and the audience was greatly augmented, the hall being filled. Mr. J. G. McMinnies, M.P., presided, and he was supported by the pastor (the Rev. J. Yonge), M. Z. Armitage, J.P., and , others. _ _ _

The CEIRaSAN, who WAS 'loudly applauded on rising, said: Ladies and gentlemen,—l need not say that lam very glad to meet you here to-night, and in such large numbers. I hope that we are all very glad to meet each other, because we meet under circumstances of great encouragement. I suppose there never was a time when this church and con- gregation existed under conditions of greater peace and prosperity. (Hear, hear.) During the last two years we have had our troubles and our fears. some of our most valued friends have been taken from us, and before they left us, I dare say, if we had been inquired of, we should have said that their absence from amongst us was seriously detrimental to this institution as a religious and educational instrumentality. But we have passed our troubles, and our fears have been dissipated; and we meet together to-night, as I said just now, under circumstances, certainly not of discouragement, but under circumstances of great hope for the future. (Applause.) We may especially con- gratulate ourselves, I think, upon the almost thorough restoration to health of our minister. (Applause.) I believe that his only weakness is his head—(laughter)—and unless he told us so I do not think that we, who are in the _ _ _ _
habit of listening to him Sunday after Sunday, would have found that out. At the same time, whatever his weakness

may be, we are very glad to see him in comparative health, and we hope to have him long amongst us, and to give us the opportunity of assuring him of our earnest sympathy and support. (Applause.) I hope that no larger sphere of usefulness—l think that is the word (laughter)—will have _ _ _

any attraction for him,and that certain rumours which have disquieted us recently have no foundation in fact. (hear, hear.) I trust that for many years we shall have him to preside over in— to preside over us as a united and attached people. (Applause.) Well, now, an occasion like this is pre-eminently a social and domestic one, and I do . . . . .

not know that it would be at all in place for either myself or anybody else to enter into any explanation or any de- fence of our peculiar principles as a denomination. We value our principles; we believe that they are connected with the spread and success of religion in this country. (Hear, hear.) But I believe I can say with the utmost cer- tainty that perhaps our denomination is one where you hear from time to time less in reference to our distinctive opinions than any other. (Hear, hear.) I remember some time ago being in London—many years ago it is now—a number of *us were staying at the same hotel, and on Sunday morn- ing we all went to wherever we desired to go—some to one place and some to another, and we assembled together again just before lunch and compared notes as to where w bad been in the morning. Some had been to this church, and that chapel, some to this cathedral and to that. A friend of mine said, "I have been to St. Paul's Cathedral." "Well," said another, "Win. did you hear 2" "Oh," said he, "I can give you the sermon in two sentences." The sermon that he had heard had really been a great magnify- ing of the principles of the Established Church; and the preacher, who was at that time the Dean of Windsor, bad made it ,quite certain to himself, and I dare say to many others, that Dissenters were at least given up t) the unco- venanted mercies of God. This friend of mine said, "I can tell you what the sermon wa, that I heard this morning in two sentences " This is the real old Eccles cake shop—(laughter) ; and none other is genuine." (Laugh- tar and applause.) Wcll, I dare say we are, and ought to be, as firmly convinced of the truth of our principles as was the Dean of Windsor. At the same time, I do not know but what we should also be disposed to say that other people may be right, and that perhaps we are not altogether right. We do not mean to say that none other is genuine; but we believe that, after all, ours is genuine. (Laughter.) Well, now, a very wise man said that there is a time for every- thing, but there are exceptions to this rule as there are to others. There is not time, for instance, to-night, for long speeches—hardly for short ones. We have je long and a very interesting programme, and I certainly shall not inter- fere between you and the enjoyment of that programme by prolonging these preliminary remarks. (Applause.) The Rev. J. YONGE afterwards rose to address the meeting.

He said—lf, sir, it affords you pleasure to be with us to- night, I am sure I am but expressing the feeling that is in every one of our hearts when I say that we are heartily glad to see you with us. (Applause.) In fact I think that Mr. McMinnies is an illustration of the right man in the right place when he takes the chair at this meeting for us year by year; and I hope most earnestly that he may be spared. under the Providence of God, for many years, not only to do this little service for us, but to render those services to this town, and to the country which he, in his capacity as one of our senators, is so well able to render. (Applause.) lam exceedingly obliged to you, sir, for the

indly way in which you m-a-,d-e reference to me in your opening remarks, and to my friends present for the cordial way in which they responded to what you have said. I do not think I should hava said anything upon the subject to which you made refer- ence, but for the fact that you led the way; and, therefore, there would be some incompleteness in what had been said if I did not fin'sh it by adding this single word, that your hopes, sir, are not likely to be disappointed at present. (Ap- plause.) lam not aware, of course, what work, what re- sponsibility, or what honour Providence may have in store for me in the future; but I do know at the present moment that nothing of the kind is within my knowledge, and that the interesting rumours, as one friend said, highly creditable to myself, which have been assiduouely circulated by some person for the past few weeks, have absolutely no foundation whatever in fact. (Applause.) I think it would be interesting if I give you a compact sketch of the last six years of your history as a church and congregation at Wycliffe. I speak of these six years because they are those in which I have :had the pleasure of knowing you. The six years during which, as people and pastor, we have been joined together, have been, as usual, years of change and vicissitude. On the whole, however, upon their review, I, for my part, am led to regard them with thankfulness; and from what the retrospect teaches I am induced to look forward with hope. I purpose to place before you in the course of a few minutes a statement of facts which I con- ceive to be encouraging in a very high degree. The six years have not been idle years. They have not been fruitless years. And 'although the fluctuations experienced have been frequently trying, and not a little suggestive of anxiety, we are to-day, on the whole, in a fairly good position, and even in some respects on a sounder basis than ever. I do not wish in this review to ignore any of the obvious facts as to our general condition, some of which have at times laid heavily upon my mind and heart. Let me observe then, at the very outset, that the numbers of our congregation, save on special occasions, appear to me to be less than was the cise six years ago. I do not know that the number of actual seat-holders is less; but the church as a rule is not so well filled as it was, although now. on Sunday evenings the attendance is usually fair. The dif- ference may be only part of the general . state of things, affecting all congregations alike. It seems to be growing fashionable to make one service a day do instead of two. In fact, in face of the small attendances in school and church on Sunday mornings, I made the other day a some- what satirical suggestion to one of our deacons that we should give up both morning school and morning service, meet in the school from 3 to 4 on Sunday afternoon, and in church from 7 to 8 in the evening, let that arrangement stand for three years, and then close the establishment altogether as obsolete and out of harmony with the spirit of the age. It must also be noted that the numbers in our Sunday school have considerably diminished. Various cir- cumstances, I think, may be mentioned ire explanation of this entire state of things. Six years ago, other churches in the town were less vigorous than they have since become. Two new congregations have during that time been formed —the Reformed Episcopal and St. Barnabas. The eause in Golborne-street has found new life under the ardent labours of our friend Mr. Mooreoand our Wesleyan friends have now for some time been rejoicing in a very effective ministry. The work at Cockhedge has also drawn away some who used to be regular worshippers, and scholars in our schools. It might be borne in mind that six years ago Cockhedge school consisted of but five teachers, and somewhat over 100 scholars; now there are 18 teachers and 430 scholars. And while the larger part of these scholars belong te that district, and did not find their way to Wycliffe school, still many did who are now attending the mission, either as teachers or scholars. I think, therefore;there is at any rate an explanation, not altogether unsatisfactory, of any diminu- tion in numbers that may be manifest. I should like, how- ever, to express a wish that among ail denominatimee, both Church and Dissent, there could be an honourable under - standing arrived at that should prevent proselytism. (Hear, hear.) The day is gone by in which sectarian rivalry should be allowed to exist. If clergy and others are anxious to fill Church schools there are hosts of children at present attached to no school, whom it would Be well to gather in. While this is the case, it is a pity to attempt to empty one school merely to fill another. There used to be a law' in England which visited with a very serious penalty such as were guilty of sheep-stealing. I think some sort of punish- ment is deserved by people who commit ecclesiastical sheep-stealing. (Applause.) And I should like to warn certain people in this town that their efforts in this direction are being watched, with a view of being defeated, if not exposed. I have now stated all the discouraging signs of our Wycliffe condition. I shall then, I think, show that they are overbalanced by other signs, which speak of growth, !consolidation, and promise fairly well for the future. Our losses during the six lyears have been considerable, and, when they are individually weighed, in cases net a few have been serious. We could not lose men like Mr. Rigby, —(applause), Mr. Murray—(applause), Mr. Blackwood— (applause), without being losers by their removal to a far

div.head: WHAT IS LIBERALISM?
div.p: WHAT IS LIBERALISM?

There is a time for everything! The present seems op- portune to consider the question, What is Liberalism ? The member for Warrington is on the eve of addressing his con- stituency ; what is of moment in this to all admirers of good government is that both member and constituency are Liberal. A few years ago this could not be said; from which we gather that time and circumstance have been effectual in giving Liberalism a local kingdom, Over which long may it dominate, to the satisfaction of the majority. The borough has no just cause to be dissatisfied with its political representative: those who have read the parlia- mentary reports, more especially the division lists, will be aware that Mr. McMinnies has earned that respect and praise which Warrington doubtless is ready to accord him; and we have grounds for believing the entente cordiale exist- ing so long between himself and Warrington Liberals will be sustained longer than the Conservative portion of the com- munity will care to witnese, or perhaps have patience to endure. Leaving the personal aspect of Mr. MicMinnies's connection with our subject, we ask: What is Liberalism? Is it a mere word, intended for no higher purpose than to dazzle and mislead? Or a vigorous literal, endorving the mlead with a sense of security in the fecund principles it represents? Is it a pretence, a subtle expression, a sham symptom of political force a something we may admire at a distance, but which on approaching we find to be a veiled skeleton, or the glamour of gilt? Or is it the important word we undestand it to be—the master key to exalting political principles? Take an analogy. Hoe is a river, in the bank beds of which at certain points stakes are driven. We conclude that a bridge is in course of construction Frequently passing, we observe the stakes multiplying with much variety of size and strength; but no bridge is formed. We should soon weary of such a haphiss affair, unless deluded into the complacent faith of people contented with the semblance of progress. Is our Liberalism like this ? Are these signs of work, of widening and extending thought, delusions ? Are the instincts of our forefathers buried impulces, and the ostensible activity 1 of current Liberalism misguiding, having no sympathy whatever with the past, whose fulness of reform and ad- vancement was as palpable and sincere as it was grand and consummate? Or are we,as a nation, borrowing energy from historic sources, arming ourselves with the tireless facility to invade where invasion means defeat to ignorance and superstition, or help to knowledge and freedom of opinion? It is only by analysis we can decide these points. We ought, as a people, if we are true to our traditions, to be on the gradient in relation to all questions. One thing, we cannot stand still. In politics, of all matters this is irre- futable. We must either grow or decay, expand or con- ' t.act, develop into glorious power, or shrink into feeble apathy. There is no intermediate state, politically speak- ing. In so vast an empire as ours, with its ceaseless call upon the Government for new laws, improvement in old ones, and destruction of obnoxious ones, we cannot have a Laodecean condition of thinge. Politics necessarily are as restless as the ocean, ever pressing on to our thronged shores, sometimes with the wild palpitation of'e e storm,,at others wi h the all but even' 'ees quiet of thva.m. Always, kowever, movire,•, always eN ILing life, ,and always impart- ing the idea of force, ve'lether in a latent or an-alert sense. How could it be otherwise, ir''eed ? So.thatewe are-corn- polled to believe we a , ei-her going forwardeor falling behind in our political eesociations. We-lemay be forced to :advance or forced to retreat: e- We cannot pause. • Conservatism, for instance, may claim to abide4.y an& •nt institutions, laws, and statutes, whieh is worsejthan standing still—equivalent to acknosv- kriging otrr 19th-centuryswisdom can be eclipsed by the un- developed, semi-barbaric brow of the 15th or 16th centuries. But we do not believe in retracing our footsteps in prostrating o arselves before the god of the )Ephesians We neither desire to turn our ftices from the sun, nor to worship the east of a yesterday! This is our day! The sun has already arisen, and we look to it as those who love light. If our Conservative or • Tory friends prefer darkness to light, the day whose sun is set to the day whose sun is mounting with brilliant strength to its throne in the heavens, we regret a taste so decidedly,retrogressional. They will pardon, at least, the next generation will applaud, our relish for pleasanter and more appropriate lodgings. The present is fed, and the future will be fattened, on the crops we are raising now. We should be famished if left to the repast a Tory government would provide. As for the future, the topic thus associated is too repellent to dwell upon. We will adjourn it for a more convenient season! The impro- bability of Toryism ever regaininee its former position • in the councils of the nation is so great that we can well afford to nod at its pretensions to the inherit- ance now in the hands of the people. Well, what is Liberalism? If the question is not a new one, if even an old one, it has neither lost that interest which attaches to subjects of moment, nor forfeited that esteem which the majority of English toilers feel towards a subject so much in sympathy with their hopes and aspira- tions. if anything, the question has deepened in interest, and preceperecl in popular esteem, as it deserves to have done. It has risen to fame; it has siezed the hearts of the people; it has wrecked the power of hereditary politieal in- fluence, at least in its most mischievious branches ; it has expanded public opinion, encouraged boldness and freedom of thought on themes once branded as State property, and given men the liberty to not only criticise the conduct of those who govern them, but the possibility of replacing the Government with one moulded to the wishes of the people, should this be necessary. It has made England what she is! For the question, "What is Liberalism?" has been for years and years an intellectual force, driving the people on to deliverance from tyranny, oppression, error, and wrong. The heroes of the past—those grand geniuses who struck the first seams of thought and intelligence which proved that England had mine after mine, rich beyond calculation, of mental ore, capable of making for her eras not iron merely, but golden. These heroes saw Liberal- ism in the crude form of a new creed, or of a picture, the maiden effort of an artist possessing the imagination, but not the skilful fingers of a Rubens. They were dazzled by the lustre which, in their enthralled eyes, made the Liberal- ism of their day not simply inviting but fascinating. Their's was but a gleam of heaven, yet it has brought sunshine to a nation. now beginning to realise how much it is indebted to these men, who instinctively grasped the sword of free- dom when the darkness of political and religious slavery rendered it utterly impossible for them to fully corre- hend the nature or value of their seizure. What is Liberalism? How many times has the question been asked since Cee first pioneer of political, and we may say religious and social reform laid his finger on the hem of the garment which now covers our people—that garment called liberty! How many! Yet every time that question has beea asked by earnest, patriotic, self-sacrificing men, one stone has been added to the construction of many decades to that "temple of liberty" which we call the House of Parliament, or more properly the House of Commons. In trying to answer the question, What is Liberalism? our thinkers have solved the

problem of political independence; or, rather, they have imposed such conditions upon us, as a people, that if the problem is not solved, it at least is in the process of solution. A generation of questioners have provoked so much mental work, have influced men to step, first with trembling footsteps, then with giant strides, to the very throne of poirer, trarorming us into a self-governing empire, that the o':.:(come is this: England to day stretches out her handi to the world, and cries—" See, hero in liberty!" P. Q. - '

div.head: ,41,:rtter to the 'editor.
div.p: ,41,:rtter to the 'editor.

"PIG AND WHISTLE," OR, " PIGA WAES-HAEL." Sir,—l crave a little more of your valuable space in con- nection with the subject that forms the heading to this letter. "Newtonian," in his communication of the Bth inst., says he has seen a certain statement in print support- ing one of the definitions I ventured to propound. He is quite correct in saying so. The following is what two youngsters I know have discovered in one of my reference books :—" This familiar tavern sign is, according to Prof. Max Milner, derived from Piga lc aee- hael , a Danish saluta- tion to the Virgin Mary." This,in fact, is the record on the subject made by Eliezer Edwards in his "Facts and phrases." May I ask "Newtonian," in the words of Milton, What boots it at one gate to make defence, And at another to let in the foe?

Or will he maintain that Professor Max Miler knows nothing about the matter? Again, see how logically, yet unconsciously, he gives opportunity for making a point or a joke. I no sooner allude to his propensity for impaling him- self on his own prongs, than he tells us his ancestors were potters. Now, the patron saint of the potters is St. Gore! And yet there are persons who assert that Scotchmen never lead up to or attempt at jokes. Catch them putting up with dry oatmeal when they come to England, if there are juicy mutton or beef to be had. I merely allude to these two facts on the obverse and reverse principle; for, granting that Zicotchmen, as a rule, are dull, we have it on the authority of Pope that "gentle dullness ever loves a joke." Trusting that this short epistle will not further irritate or disturb " Newtonian " mwng, I beg to remain, Sir, Sc., sNGLO-SCOTUS. Newington, London, S.E., Jan. 13.

The friction of d pulley was the cause of the out- break, and, on account of the flames spreading so rapidly, several operatives lost their clothes, while others were partially suffocated, and two—Hopkins and Wigham—had to be attended by a doctor. The flames were confined to snfroom, but the contents of four floors were rendered al- most useless by water. The property is insured. FATAL FIRE AT MANciumaa.—On Wednesday night a fire, occurred in a dwelling-house occupied by Joseph Levenstein, 8, Park-street, Cheetharn, Manchester. Two children were in'bed in a mailroom on the first floor. When thelast Was put' to rest by Mrs. Isevenstein, she put a lighted candle near a basket of clothes, which, it is supposedebecame ignited. Soon after she had gone downstairs she heard a cry, and on going upstairs she found the room on fire. She rescued one child—a boy six years of age—who, however, ' was badly burnt; but the other—a boy of two years—was burnt to a cinder. 31ANY PERSONS BITTEN 13YA DOG.—For Some time on Tuesday night the town of Garston, near Liverpool, was in a great commotion owing to the ravages of a mad dog which scoured the streets, biting men, women, and children as he passed along. The police were busy following him from street to street till midnight, when he was lost sight of. One of the County Constabulary, named Fox, procured a double-barrelled gun and Wowed the track of the dog until five o'clock on Wednesday morning, when he found the animal in a garden' crouching under a hedge and howl- ing hideously. The policeman at once shot the dog, It had bitten a number of persons at Woolton, One of the persons bitten rather severely is Mr. J. Pilkington, veterinary sur- geon, Garston. div.head: ALLEGED TRESPASS IN PURSUE' OF GAME AT PENKETIT,
div.p: ALLEGED TRESPASS IN PURSUE' OF GAME AT PENKETIT,

On Wednesday, at Warrington County Petty Sessions before Messrs. P. Stubs, Z. Armitage, and J. Manion, Philip Forshaw was summoned for trespassing in pursuit of game on land in the occupation of Mr. Alfred Bennett. at Pen- keth, on Friday, the Bth December.—Mr. Percy Davies appeared for the defendant, and pleaded not guilty. He remarked that he was glad he appeared in the case, as it gave him the opportunity of congratulating Messrs. Armi- tage and Matson on their first appearance OH the bench as magistrates for the county of Lancaster, and he hoped that he, as a professional man, would have as much pleasure in appearing before them as he had had before Mr. Stubs and other magistrates.—P.C. Rogers then stated that at about nine o'clock on the day in question he saw the defendant on the field at Penketh belonging to Mr. Bennett. Defendant had a dog and gun with him, and as soon as he noticed witness was watching him he ran away.—Mr. P. Davies: Are you quite sure that you saw the defendant in the field on the Bth Dec.?—Witness: Yes.—Mr. Davies: How is it that you never took out the summons until the 9th inst., when the trespass is alleged to have taken place on the Bth December? Witness: Because Mr. Baring's keeper had gone to Lsndon P—Mr. Davies: When did he go to London? —Witness: I do not know.—Mr. Davies: Was it a fine day on the Bth December 2—VVitness : Yes; it was a fine frosty morning.—Mr. Davies: What time did you see the defend- ant ?—Witness: About nine o'clock in the morning, as I was going down to the station.--Mr. Davies stated that defendant did not leave his house on that day until eleven o'clock in the morning, and hrthad five witnesses to prove where he was the whole of the day. The policeman had stated that it was a fine frosty morning on the Bth December, whereas it was a very foggy morning, and defendant being a delicate man did not go out at all until a Mr. Branwood, who car- ries on business in Warrington, called for him in his cart, and he was in Mr. Branwood's company until two o'clock in the afternoon.—Mr. Stubs said that as the offence was stated to have been committed at nine o'clock in the morning no evidence needed to be gone into regarding what took place after 11 o'clock.—Mr. Davies stated that no time was mentioned in the summons, and he had come prepared to prove where the defendant was the whole of the day. He then called defendant's wife, but Mr. Stubs said he did not think Mr. Davies had any right to call the wife to give evi- dence, and he asked Mr. Buckton (the magistrates clerk) if it was not so.—Mr. Buckton: I think he has. What do you say ?—Mr. Davies : You are the clerk to the magis- trates, and you will advise the magistrates as to whether I have the power or not. I think you will allow that I have power in a case of trespass.—Defendant's wife then stated that her husband never left the house until 11 o'clock, and never had his gun in his hand at all on the day named. Mrs. Clare, a neighbour of hers, was in the house, and saw the defendant there between 9 and II o'elock.—Mr. Buckton then very closely cross-examined the witness, when Mr. Davies interrupted him and protested against the conduct of the clerk, stating that 'the course he was taking was most unjustifiable, and that the clerk was putting words into her mouth, and making use sf language that he had no right to do.—The Clerk: When you have been as long in practice as I have Mr. Davies, interrupting, said it was perfect nonsense to conduct a court of justice in this manner, and that he had had far more experience and practice than Mr. Buckton had in a police court.—Mr. Stubs said the Bench would have asked the question if Mr. Buckton had not.—The witness was then further cross-examined by Mr. Buckton, but her evidence was not shaken.—Mr. Davies then called Mrs. Clare, who lives next door to the defendant, and she also gave evidence corroborative of the statement made by the last witness.—Mr. Baring's gamekeeper, then came forward, and asked that the case might be adjourned in order to get more evidence.—Mr. Davies said it would be establishing a precedent indeed, if the case was adjourned under the present circumstances. He had five witnesses present who had come to give evidence, and the prosecutor ought to have been prepared. His client was charged with trespassing in pursuit of game on the Bth December, and he had five witnesses to prove where he was on that day, and to show that he never was in the field in quebtion, or in pursuit of game. It was a very wrong application, and the magistrates ought not to enter- tain it for a moment, for if an adjournment was granted he should have a perfect right, on behalf of his client, to ask for another adjournment to bring further witnesses to dis- prove what was said at the adjourned hearing of the case. He protested against the way in which the case had been conducted, and he wished it to go to the public that the course which this gentleman was now taking had come from the clerk. The clerk had advised the magistrates that the prosecutor ough to apply to the Bench for an adjournment. The bench then instructed the clerk to ask prosecutor to make the applications. The clerk turned round to the police-ser- geant and gave him a message to deliver to the prosecutor, the sergeant gave the message to P.C. Rogers, and he walked round the court and gave it to the prosecutor, and the prose- cutor was now making the application. He protested that that was an unfair way to conduct a prosecution.—Mr. Buck- ton stated that the prosecutor, if the case was not adjourned, could take out another summons.—Mr. Davies said he would not object to that, but the case ought to be dismissed.—The magistrates consulted, and ultimately dismissed the case.

We (Mandarcl) are authorised to state that no date has yet been definitely fixed for the enthronement of the Arch- bishop Designate in Canterbury Cathedral. The ceremony will, however, take place as soon after Easter as possible. Mr. Gladstone, accompanied by Mrs. Gladstone, left Lon- don on Wednesday morning, and crossed ever to Calais. The sea passage was a fine one, and Mr. Gladstone rtmained on the bridge the whole of the time. At Calais the train was taken for Paris, which latter city the travellers passed through without halting, on their way to Cannes, which was reached in the evenifig, Sir Stafford Northcote, it is stated, is deriving so much benefit from the sea air that he will prolong his trip till February.

div.head: EMMANUEL CITURCII BAZAAR.
div.p: EMMANUEL CITURCII BAZAAR.

Rapid Progress is being made in the erection of Emmanuel Reformed Church, the memorial stones of which were laid under the most favourable auspices early in October last; and before very long the edifice, which is already beginning to show signs of completion, will form a handsome addition to the architecture of Bold-street. The structure will cost some £2,000, and towards this amount the congregation have raised about £6OO, and, with a view to further increas- ing the fund for liquidating the debt, they had adopted a popular expedient and promoted a bazaar. Considerable preparation had been made for the bazaar, which was held in the Warrington Public Hall this week, and extended over three days. It was opened in the presence of a large number of visitors on Wednesday afternoon, when the hall possessed a pleasing appearance. The numerous trophies of bright flags that adorned the gallery tended to increase the attractiveness of the goods so invitingly displayed on the several stalls placed round the hall. Nowhere, perhaps, has the advancement of the public taste in art been so apparent as at bazaars, and in the present instance the artistic skill exhibited in the design and execution of many of the articles was of a high order. Indeed, most of the goods were of a superior description, and while there was an extensive collection of what are des- cribed as ornamental, there was an equally large array of serviceable things, in the execution of which much time had been expended. Beaded bannerettes, Turkish cushions, crewel-worked cushions and cosies, Japanese ware glass lower vases, toilet tidies, work baskets, small bags of flour, a pair of clogs, (tic., occupied conspicuous positions of the stall next the door, which also contained a large quantity of children's clothing. The stall was under the superintendence of Miss Allen, Miss M. E. Hindley, and Miss Gandy. Among the principal articles on the next stall, in charge of Mrs. Galloway, Mrs. Page, Mrs. Knowles, and Miss Shepherd, may be mentioned a beautiful marble clock, splendid brackets and stands in leather, a handsome raised wool work cushion, capital water-colour drawings, dolls' beds and cradles, a beautiful velvet and satin bed quilt, a patchwork satin bed quilt (worked by a gentleman in four years' leisure hours), patchwork and needlework cushions, a variety of antimacassars and children's frocks, hand-painted terracotta, dic. Mrs. Lowe, Mrs. Hesketh, and Miss Sutton presided over the third stall, which stood under the centre gallery. In front of it was the mottoe "Success to the Emmanuel Reformed Church of England Bazaar, Warrington ;" and placed in prominent positions were wool and crewel worked satin cosies, crewel worked brackets, painted and worked "chair backs," beaded footstools, a neat wicker work draw- ing room chair covered with . needlework, artistic outline antimacassars, large water colour draw- ings, coal vases, dolls' bed, hand painted terra cotta, and a quantity of wearing apparel. On the fourth stall were exhibited scholastic materials from Scotland, plush picture frames, a pretty dolls' bed made of marple, Japanese trays, menu cards, a patch-work quilt (the work of a gentleman), dolls, baskets, and a large assortment of wearing apparel and underclothing. In charge of this stall were Mrs. Howard, Mrs. H.elsby, Mrs. Buckley, and Mrs. Blackburn. A portrait of Her Majesty the Queen was conspicuous in front of the sixth stall superintended by Mrs. Mules, Mrs. Hall, Mrs. Parsons, and Mrs. Jewkes; and attention was also arrested by a crewel-worked Boren on,, a bamboo cane frame, a mahogany whatnot, tapestry work, I painted brackets, footstools, Chinese soap stone trays, hand I painted vases and antimacassars, tapestry table cloth, I knitted cotton cradle cover, crewel-worked toilet sets, fire screen with pen and ink ornamentation, terra cotta work, leather brackets and numerous other articles. Mrs. Spinks had charge of the scholars' stall, which chiefly contained plain needlework, children's clothing, toys, &c.; while the tempting refreshment stall was under the manage- ment of Mrs. Burrows. Below the platform was a miniature model of the Manchester Ship Canal, on whose waters floated several craft and -water fowls, and on one bank were numerous "cattle" grazing in front of farmhouses, the other being set apart for the working of a model steam engine. There was also an exhibition of curiosities and works of art well worthy of patronage. It comprised cork models of Walton Church (built by Sir G. Greenall), War- rington Parish Church and St. Paul's Church, Southport (by Mr. Rudd, a Latchford grocer) ; facsimiles of Magna Charts, of warrants to execute Mary, Queen of Scots, and King Charles I. • also of the declaration of independence of U. S. America (1776) ; the arms, names, and titles of all the peers of England to the year 1768, and other rare and interesting papers containing records of various important historical events, besides a collection of rare coins, and specimens of taxidermy and fret work. The ceremony of opening the bazaar was performed by Mr. R. A. Naylor, who was supported by the Rev. W. Mules, Mr. Z. Armitage, J.P., and Mr. Thomas Woods. In a brief address Mr. Naylor
_ referred to the popularity of bazaars, and expressed his willingness to help that bazaar to the extent of £lO, after which he declared the bazaar open, and the sales commenced.
CHARGE AGAINST A RUNCORN BOATBUILDER'S WIFE.

At Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. W. Bankes and Mr. S. B. Chadwick, Sarah Stubbs, a married woman, was brought up on remand charged with having, on the 15th instant, feloniously stolen 7t yards of print, the property of Robert Rob:arts.—Mr. Burton defended the prisoner.—The prosecuta said he was a draper, and occu- pied a shop at the bottu'in of Ellesmere-street. On Monday evening last he was holding a, sale of drapery goods at his shop. He did not sell any print by auction or privately. The print produced was his property. Between eight and nine o'clock on Monday night Mrs. Kelly, wife of a con- stable, who was in the shop, told him that a woman had stolen a piece of print, and he whistled. Two officers came up, and he gave information to them. The print was worth ss.—By Mr. Burton: Dress goods were being sold in the sitting-room. The shop was full of people, and the sale that night realised £2O, made up of small items. He was in the sitting-room once. He and the assistant handed the articles to the auctioneer. The auctioneer was standing near some prints, and if he had wanted to take one up for saie he could have done so. When he was told a piece,oferint had been taken he did not say it was a piece ofp3Pottethprint. worth 103 6d. ' He was selling the goods because,hi harhad short • notice' to leave 'the premises.— Evan Williams, assistant to the, prosecutor, stated,that the int-produced-belonged to Mr. Roberts. He had made the figure on:the ticket which was attached.' ~ He did not see any printput up, and he would swear,.that none.was put up. He was not, present the whole-of the time during which the isale was going on.—By Mr.:Burton : He cut scores oW'ress -pieces ..np in the back shop.—Ellen Kelly, wife of,P.C. Kelly, said she • was at the sale on Mond ty evening last.The,prisoner was there, standing, behind her. A piece of printifell off the side of the window on to the floor, passing on to the witness's shoulder. and 2down • her back, and she thought 7the prisoner would get,- it into her hands, and • put it back again, but-she did not actually see.the prisoner get hold-of it. The pint had a white stripe like the one produced.—Mr. John- son: Then what you said yesterday morning,that•you.saw her put it under her shawl is not correct ? Witness: She. must have put it under -her ,--shawl.—Mr. Johnson:' But did you see her. Witness No ;, but-I could swear she put it under.—By Mr. Burton: - Shenever saw the print in the possession of the prisoner.—Barnett Dutton, auctioneer,carry- ing on lansiness,at Widnes, deposed that he was selling at the prosecutor's shop on Monday evening last. He did not sell anyprint thatnight. He had 'a small piece of print put into his hand to,sell, • but nt was put down again.—By Mr. Burton: He sold sonierstriped galatia.,— P.C:Finney stated that from information received, he went' to the pri- soner's hcuse in Grove-street. on Monday night. He told the prisoner she was suspected of stealing a-piece of prin. She said " I have got a piece here, but I hought4t. I gave 2s. 4d. for He then took-her-into custody, and, in an- swer to the charge, she.said, "I didn't steal it. I bought-it. I gave him half-a-crown, and -t the young man in the shop gave me 2d. out of it."—By -Mr. Burton: There was also. a piece of muslin on the dresser, where he got the print pro- duced from. There - was no _attempt . at concealment. The prisoner elected to -be. tried by the magistrates, and Mr. Burton, in'hivaddress,.said the prisoner was-the wife of Peter Stubbs,rla boatbuilder, an aged and respectable man. She had been his wife for 30 -years, and during the greater proporcion of that time they had lived in Runcorn, where not a single person up to the present time had pointed the finger of scorn at her. He would call evidence which would completely rebut the accusation made against the prisoner, and he should ask their worships to say that the charge was without foundation, that the prisoner had not been guilty I of the charge brought against her, and that she left that I court without a stain upon her character. It was a charge which ought not to have been brought before the Bench or before any court of justice.—Elizabeth Dagnall, wife ot John Dagnall, of Robert-street, Halton-road, was then called. She said she was at the sale from seven o'clock until a little before eleven on Monday night. There were three lots of galatia sold, and she saw the auctioneer take up a fourth and offer it, but no one would bid, and he put it down. A woman, named Mary Jane Antrobus, asked the auctioueer to put up the piece of print produced, and he did so, saying "it is over seven yards, but we will call it seven." Ayoung manynamed Williams bid a shilling, jocularly remarking that it would do for potato bags. The prisoner bid is 2d, and witness is 7d, and eventually it was knocked down at 2s 4d to the prisoner. The prisoner paid the assistant, who gave her some change; she could not tell the amount. The prisoner at that time had some muslin curtains on her arm. Near her was a heap of flannel, and upon it she placed the print and the muslin. About half an hour someone said she was wanted, and called her out. She reached her things from the place where she had nut them, and placed them over her shawl on her arm. In crushing through the crowd of persons around her, she dropped one of the articles, but the witness could not say whether it was print or muslin. Someone told Mr. Roberts a person had taken a piece of print, and he came and looked at the pile, then saying the piece taken was spotted print worth 10s 6d. Mr. Roberts was in and out of the shop all night.— Eliza Cook, wife of William Cook, of Halton-road; Mary Jane Antrobus, wife of Frank Antrobus, of 58, NeLson-street,

gave evidence strongly confirming this statement, and Mr. Banks said the Bench were of opinion there was no cise,t° go before a jury, and that there was not the slightest Staill upon the prisoner's character.—Mr. Barton: That there blit been a gross miscarriage of justice—Mr. Banks: I dot go so far as that. She will be discharged. (APPIIIIIS4 Which was immediately silenced.)
