STONERS. THE WATERLOO HOUSE QUESTION. MR. SHAW ON FRAUD. An adjourned meeting of the Runcorn Board of Com- missioners, was held at the Town Hall, on Wednesday even- ing, for the purpose of receiving the report of the committee sP tp ointed to consider the best means of utilizing Waterloo House. There were present Dr. Steele (chairman), Messrs. Norman, Fisher, Williams, P. Speakman, Meadowcroft, Pritchard, Rhodes, Shaw, Taylor, Lake, Lightburn, Linaker (law-clerk), and B _rockes (secretary.) Tne CHAIRMAN "said he had just been told that Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst desired to speak with the Board before they discussed the matter in any way.—Mr. SHAW said he did not see that anything that could be said by any outsider ought to interfere with the Board in the fair discussion of the question. Except the Board could coincide with certain views he might entertain, it would not be nice to discuss the matter with Mr. liazie- hurst.—The CHAIRMAN said he would not permit the Board to be driven. but he thought it would be courteous to give Mr. Hazlehurst an interview. Mr. SHAW thought the Board ought to hear no remarks from Mr. Hazlehurst, before the Board had received the committee's report.—Mr. LAKE said Mr. Hazleburst was not exactly an outsider because the removal to Waterloo House was con- nected with the Library, and also with Mr. Hazlehurst's offer, and the arrangements at Waterloo House might have some effect upon that offer. The offer was made perfectly open, leaving every arrangement to the committee. It was well known that the general opinion of the Board was in favour of certain rooms and there could be no possible ob- jection to hearing what Mr. Hezlehurst had to say.—Mr. SHAW: I should certainly object if Mr. Hazlehurst was to come to that Board and say "Except you do what I want shall Rot subscribe a penny to the Library."—The LAW CLERK: Why not hear what he has to say and make no comment.—Mr. MsartowcnorT thought an interview with Mr. Hazlehurst would interfere with a free, full, and im- partial consideration of the question.—Mr. NORMAN : I don't think there can be any harm in hearing what Mr. Hazle- burst has to say.—The CHAIRMAN: I don't think so.—Mr. &raw said they did not want Mr. Hazlehurst to enter into any argument as to the arrangement of the rooms in Waterloo House. He did not think he ougnt to come and say, "If you don't give me this, then I shan't give you this," be- cause it detracted from the dignity of the Board. Either the Board had a right to discuss this question or they had not.—Mr. LAKE said it did not affect their right to discuss the question—Mr. FISHER did not think the Board had any right to take Mr. Hazlehurst's offer into consideration at all. —Mr. Hazlehurst was then called into the room by direc- tion of the Chairman, who requested the reporters to retire. The private interview ended, Mr. SHAW read the Committee's report which stated that in accordance with the desire of the Board, the committee bad very carefully considered the question of providing accommodation at Waterloo House for the library, daily reading room, and Commissioners' offices; and their report they ventured to think would meet with the Board's appro- val. They were not laying before them plans of a proposed building for the purposes mentioned, but, with materials at command, to provide suitable and convenient accommoda- tion' first for the books, secondly for the readers, thirdly for the borrowers, and lastly for the offices of this Board, Jet. The book space in the Commissioners' present board-room, which was considered by the Library Committee suitable for their requirements, contains 600 feet, and the remaining space for readers 300 feet. They merely teferred to this plan so that the members might be able to compare the space here with that in the rooms they thought suitable at Waterloo House. The rooms to the right side of the entrance hall (as you face inwards) were those proposed for the library. The reading-room was the first one approached, I being of the following dimensions : 357 superficial feet of I floor space. As compared with the space allotted for readers in the present Board-room, namely, 300 feet, they had 57 feet more in the proposed room than in this one. The next room which they would call the book room, gave wall space for books of 478 feet. An- other room, leading out of this, as an additional book-room, contained wall space of 340 feet, and a double stand near the side for books would be equal to 120 feet, so that taking these last two rooms together they had 938 feet of book space as against 600 feet in the present Board-room, or in other words, we have 338 feet more space in the proposed rooms than in that one. So much for the space for books and for readers. The committee attached great importance to the facilities these rooms give over the other suggested, for enabling the very large number of borrowers to change their books, and the convenience to readers for examination of catalogues, obtaining books, and for quiet reading, as there would be no disturbance whatever caused by the librarian in changing books, tic. In the proposed rooms there would be no necessity of having to close the reading- room whilst about 700 borrowers change their books, or, what would be equivalent to closint the reading-room, attempting the impossible task of changing the borrowers' books from the reading-room during the time it is open for readers, without very great inconvenience and annoyance, and which, they felt sure, would ultimately lead to the closing of the room during the process of changing. A great advantage to the borrowers also was that they would be able to change their books without crush or inconvenience; this could be done by putting a sliding window to the wall of the library, running parallel with the front entrance hall, where a desk let into the wall, for catalogues and slips for borrowers, would be pro- vided similar to the one in the reading room. The commit- tee felt that they could not too strongly recommend to the notice of the Board the importance of the librarian being able, as in this case, to have full command of the reading- room, as well as the advantage of the public being able to 'Change their books at any time during the day without dis- turbing the readers, or inconvenience to the librarian, and if there be any drawbacks to the scheme (and of course there must be some, as the rooms were not built for the purpose of a library), they thought they were counterbalanced by the many advantages referred to. Now they would explain how the rooms on the other side of the hall would be utilised :—No. 1 was the front room, containing 200 super- ficial feet of the floor space, and excellently adapted for the secretary's office. A double desk could be placed between the two windows, thus having light on each side of the desk, at which either four or six clerks could be accommodated. No. 2, containir'oe 550 superficial feet of floor space, would make the Board Room, and there was no doubt about it being the most suitable room in the house for the purpose. By making a door in the wall which separates the room from the secretary's, the secretary would be in direct com- munication with the Board, without being obliged to go out into the passage. They would ale° observe a recess in the wall referred to, which would hold the surveyor's plan case, so that it would be close at hand when required. The table, as planned in this room, being in the form of a horse shoe, would give a great deal more sitting room than they had at present, and would also enable every member of the Board to be almost face to face with the cheirrnan. No. 3 room could be fitted as a lavatory with every convenience for the use of the Commissioners, and the small room at the end would serve as a store room for the secretary. Nos. 4 and 5 would be two rooms for the surveyor, the former being very spacious, thus affording him comfortable quarters instead of being cramped up as he was at present. In fact, if they had to build premises for the purpose they could not choose a better model than the one the above six rooms gave. Nos. 6 and 7 would be convenient for the caretaker as sit- ting room and kitchen respectively. Having thus disposed of the ground floor, they would now state how they should propose to allot the suites of rooms on the floor above : Those two rooms above the library suite could be allotted to the School Board, and would answer their purposes in every respect, giving them better accommodation than they had at present. Opposite these rooms, and immediately over the secretary's and the Board room was a handsome suite of two rooms, which could be allotted to the Overseers, and suit admirably all their requirements. The other rooms on the same floor would give ample accommodation as bed- rooms, Arcs for the caretaker. The report concluded as fol- lows :—We will first, as an example, take Waterloo House as equivalent to a rental of £BO per annum, which amount, added to a low rental value of £25 per annum for these rooms, will give us a total of £lO5 per annum to debit our- selves. Against this amount we should fix the rents of Waterloo House as follows :—The Commissioners' rooms, being so far superior to our present ones, would be well worth £4O per annum. The School Board suite we should fix at the moderate sum of £25 per annum. The Overseer's rooms we should also fix at £25 per annum. These low rentals cannot fail to give them satisfac- tion, when they bear in mind the extra accom- modation they will have in these splendid premises. The library suite we will put down at the modest sum of £25 per annum to give us a basis upon which to work. On adding the above amounts together it will give us a total of £ll5 to credit as against the former amount of £lO5 to our debit, making a surplus of £lO to our credit, which aineunt we purpose dealing with as follows :—On taking possession of their rooms by either the Overseers or School Board, we should credit the Library Committee with an extra £5 per annum, and on the remaining suite of rooms being let, an extra £5 per annum would also be credited to them, thus reducing the nominal charge to the library to £l5 a year, or, in other words, we should hand them over the sum of £155 from the amount ef £l7O we receive yearly from the rates for the purposes of the library. We have now endea- voured to show you how we can realise £lO5 per annum from the premises in Waterloo-road, charging the several bodies before referred to, moderate rents for the premises allotted to them, leaving y„ ifthe i.t pfroersenzt2sCopmemr isasnionnuemrs: offiees to 'deal with, which, would be so much clear gain to the ratepayers of Runcorn, after providing excellent and suitable accommodation, in , the first place, for the purposes of the Library, secondly the Commissioners, thirdly, the School Board, and lastly, the Overseers, as well as providing ample accommodation for a caretaker to live on the premises. In conclusion, gentle- men, we have great pleasure in recommending this report to your kind consideration, and trust that after due delibera- tion you will see your way to its adoption.—Mr. &Law moved the adoption of tbe report, and Mr. FISHER se- conded, he latter gentleman remarking that if the scheme, as presented, were adopted by the Board, they would be doing one of the best things for Runcorn that had been done for a great length of time. The committee had gone into the matter thoroughly, and had tried to utilize the house in many ways, but they could find no better way than the one presented. Financially, it was a good speculation, the ratepayers being saved about £6O or £7O a year, besides being able to supply the wants of all the public offices in I the town for 15 or 20 years at least.—The CHAIRMAN read the resolution passed on August 9th, which was to the effect that the present offices be let, and that when so le part of Waterloo House be set apart for the offices of th

Board, and part for the Free Library the remainder of the building to be let on a tenancy. He pointed out that this presented no difficulty to the Commissioners removing at ence.—Mr. LAKE suggested that the clauses in the report referring to rentals should be left out; but the LAW CLERK said the adoption of the report did not bind the Board. They could deal with the rentals by any resolution after- wards.—Mr. SUAW said Mr. Lake had referred to the tin- certainty which existed as to whether the Cc mmissioners could charge the Free Library Committee a rent or not. It , would be well to allow uncertainty to exist no longer. What the Law Clerk stated was quite clear ; that if the Commissioners pay the Library Committee £l7O per annum, that committee could please itself whether it returned any of that amount or not. That, an the face of it, did not carry what was right or what was law on the matter. The Commissioners had power to pay the Library Committee any proportion of the £l7O they thought proper, withholding any amount they thought proper for the pur- poses of carrying out the Act. Therefore, what the com- mittee here recommended was perfectly legitimate.—Mr. RFIODES remarked that this was not a question for them to discuss at the present time.—At the request of Mr. LAKE, the minute appointing the Committee re Waterloo House was read, and he said that part of the report dealing with rent did not come within that minute. There was an im- poetant principle involved in the proposition to deduct any amount from the Library rate. He maintained that the Library was too poor to pay anything.—Mr. NORMAN: Go for relief to the Workhouse.—Mr. LAKE: I don't think the Board by a side wind ought to quietly charge a rent. I think the question ought to come on its own merits.—The CHAIRMAN said the Board had no right to give the Library Committee £l7O and rooms, and they could not without being surcharged by the auditor.—Mr. LAKE moved that that part of the report referring to rent be omitted—Mr. PRITCHARD seconded, because he sym- pathised with the members of the Free Library Committee, who thought a rent ought not to be charged, and he con- sidered they ought not to commit (The LAW CLERK: You are committing yourselves to nothing)—them to do so by adopting that report in full. He also objected to those clauses on account of the School Board, of which he was a member, because be should not like them to be committed to that amount of rent, which practically they would be if they adopted that report.—Mr. MEADOWCROFT thought the report would not have been complete without some reference to the weight with which Waterloo House hanged now upon the Commissioners. They paid about £BO a year interest, and the committee showed how the ratepayers might be re- lieved. The committee did not say that the Commissioners were absolutely bound by the figures, but he should be pre- pared at any time to maintain that the Library Committee ought to pay a rent for the use of the rooms.—Mr. LIGHT- BURN obeerved that he fully concurred in the proposed divi- sion of the building, but he could not agree with that part of the report dealing with rent.—Mr. SHAW remarked that he could not express his abhorrence of the assertion that the Board could run outside of an Act of Parliament to commit a fraud upon the ratepayers and take from them something that they had no right to do, and which the law said they should not. He could not be a party to that on any consideration. He trusted that at the present time, when it was within their knowledge that hundreds of rate- payers in the town were struggling from disease that had been visiting their homes, and they had scarcely wherewith to provide the necessities of life, they would not at the in- stigation of any committee go and take from them some- thing which the law said they should. He could be no party to that—(hear, hear)—and while they thought that the reasons that some persons had opposed the Library going beyond its legitimate lines had been because it took so much from wealthy ratepayers pockets, he said every gentleman at that Board was responsible for the poorest ratepayer in the town, and they had the right, as conscien- tious, honest men, to do no act that should rob these poor men that were struggling with their families by fraudulent means.—Mr. LAKE : I rather object to this course. It strikes me as being hardly in order.—Mr. SHAW: The Act states clearly that for the purpose of carrying on the Free Library the rate shall not exceed Id. in the £, and when gentlemen want you to devote other money belonging. to the ratepayers for the purposes of the Act, you are to that extent defrauding the people. I shall be very pleased if any gentleman will show me that•it is not fraud.—Mr. LIGHTBURN : Will yJu show necessity for the charge.— Mr. Shaw reiterated his statement, and Mr. Lightburn rose to his feet to make a speech, when the Chairman declared that he was out of order, and put the amendment, for which four voted. The original motion received the sup- port of six members, and was declared carried.—lt was then decided on the motion of Mr. SHAW, seconded by Mr. MEADOWCROFT, that the report be printed at a cost not ex- ceeding 205., and the meeting terminated.

div.head: WIDNES LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WIDNES LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.

The annual meeting of the members of the East Divisioa of the Widnes Liberal Association was held at the Albert Hc>tel, Appleton, on Tuesday evening, under the presidency of Mr. Joseph Morrison. The minutes of the last meeting having been read by Mr. H. B. Shores, the secretary, and confirmed, the General Committee was constituted as follows, on the motion of Mr. NEWALL, seconded by Mr. COSIER :—Messrs. J. L. Muspratt, T. Cosier, D. Wright, R. Fogg, J Hamblett, S. Kidd, S. Robinson, P. Fallon, D. Hirst, T. Deakin, F. Hurter, C. 3tout, A. Speakman, J. W. Carlile, W. H. Kershaw, W. Pritchard, J. Leathwood, J. W. Wareing, A. Poulson, J. Leathgrbarrow, J. Y. Dale, J. W. Davies, J. Horabin, S. K. Muspratt, Jos. Morrison, J. Davies, J. H. Lewis, R. Mercer, G. Rae, D. Forster, T. Bennett, A. Cawley, J. Brock, A. Walker, W. Hartley, J. Hargreaves, W. Doward, jun., J. Newall, Daniel Stows, and W. Mountield, Mr. COSIER moved, and Mr. D. WRIGIIT seconded, a pro- position that the following gentlemen be the Executive Committee :—Joseph Morrison, George Rae, D. Wright, J. W. Carlile, D. Hirst, S. Robinson, J. Hamblett, T. Cosier, R. Fogg, W. Doward, jun. The motion was carried.

A letter was read from Mr. J. W. Davies, resigning his position as hon. secretary. The CHAIRHAN moved that the resignation of Mr. Davies be accepted, and that a hearty vote of thanks be accorded to him for his past services. Mr. COSIER seconded the proposition, which was carried. Mr. George Rae was, on the proposition of Mr. CostEß, seconded by Mr. D. WRIGHT, appointed to the vacant post. Mr. WRIGHT proposed that the meeting tender its best thanks to the chairman for his services during the past year, and that he be re-elected to that position during the coming year. Mr. Wright remarked that the members 'had always found Mr. Morrison a gentleman in every respect, and he believed that he was heart and soul in the work.
Mr. RAE seconded the motion, which was unanimously carried.

The CHAIRMAN, in reply, said he must thank those present for their kind vote of thanks, and also for again appointing him their chairman for the ensuing year. He must confess that he felt somewhat ashamed of the little the committee did last year. They would remember that they met in that house, and that some of those then present undertook to see certain peop'e, obtain certain information, and report to the secretary in time for the revision. But he believed that was not done. The result was that the secre- tary had to get the iuformation himself. That Mr. Shores did his part of the work was shown by the great success the party gained at the Revision Court, and he thought it showed the advantage of engaging a gentleman of ability, a gentleman who thoroughly understood the work, and whose heart and soul was in it. He might safely say that the whole of the work of the revision last year fell upon the shoulders of the vice-president (Mr. Carey) and Mr. Shores. He knew that Mr. Carey spent many evenings with Mr. Shores in goingover the list of voters name by name in order that it might be complete, and he felt certain that Liberalism in this district owed much to Mr. Carey for acting as the guiding spirit in the important work of organisation, for depend upon it, the work of revision of votes was an important work in Liberal organisation. During the next year, or be- fore the next election, he thought they would have the borough franchise extended to the counties. The number of voters would then be enormously increased, and the work of the committee would be proportionately increased, and he hoped they in Widnes would be prepared to do their share of the work. If they only did their duty they would be able to return a Liberal fcr this part of South-West Lanca- shire. He believed there was a great future before the Liberal party, and he should like to see the Widnes organi- sation doing something in the way of educating the people in the true principles of Liberalism. He was confident there were many intelligent Conservatives who were tired of a passive policy. They knew that if this country was' to hold its own there were certain abuses which must be swept away and certain reforms which must be instituted in order that the resources of the country might be utilised to the best possible extent. There must be a reform in the land laws; the transfer of land must be made cheaper and easier; law procedure must be revised. For instance, the case that had just recently taken place in London—the Belt case—which occupied a court of law for weeks and weeks. That was scandalous to the country; the case ought to have been settled in a few days. A reform in county government was necessary and must come. He was perfectly certain that the people who had charge of the local affairs of this country were getting sick of the interference of the Local Government Board in London. (Hear, hear.) They knew that a certain amount of revision was required, but, still, the "red tapeism " which wewt on in London was perfectly scandalous. Mr. Wright had had something to do with the Local Board of Widnes, and was aware of the trouble they had. He (Mr. Morrison) did think that Board could rule a book without having to send it to London to be approved. (Hear, hear.) What was the work of the Local Government Board control worth. They knew that they sent auditors about the country every year at a vast expense ; but not- withstanding this precaution, there was about four years ago the Local Board of Oswaldtwistle in Lancashire robbed of about £42,000. These were abuses which ought not to exist, and there was no doubt a radical reform required in the Local Government Board. It was almost impossible for anybody to say what his rates were. He was perfectly certain he could not tell what his rates amounted to in a. year. There was the Local Board rate, poor rate, income tax and household duty all col- lected by different men at different -times and he believed the Board of Guardians could 'lay a poor rate as often as they liked. It was not an annual rate, they just.lev,ed it when they wanted the money. Take again elections in the country. They had elections for members of Parliament, of local boards, of boards of guardians, and of school boards, and they wern nearly all different, sometimes they voted by ballot, sometimes by papers, and sometimes they had a single vote, and sometimes a plurality of votes.

RENT AND "PRIVATE TAXING." Dr. STEELE complained that he had been misreported at the last meeting, and he had written the following correc- tion :—As far as I am aware, that with one exception (I al- lude to Mr. Simpson), we members of the Library Committee, professing to have the interests of the Library at heart, have been very chary of dipping into our own pockets though we have been ready enough to allow the ratepayers to be taxed another penny in the pound. I say we should show our interest by subscribing among oueselves the equivalent of the amount which will be deducted by the Commissioners in lieu of rent, so as not to cripple the library funds. lam willing to do my share, and will, for one year at least, subscribe the sum [£s) I mentioned, provided the other members of the committee (excluding Mr. Simpson, who has already been so generous,) will make up the balance.—The CHAIRMAN said he should object on principle to any proposition which made the members of a committee, who gave their time and troable, responsible for any extra payments. He did not object to give a proportion, but to the geveral principle.— Mr. SIMPSON: I quite agree with that.—Mr. MEADOWCROFT remarked that it was at first stated that a halfpenny rate, which would produce £B5 a year, would be sufficient, and it was now stated that £l7O a year would not do. If they went on increasing in the manner proposed by Dr. Steele, which he termed private taxing, he did not know where they would be landed.—The Board then separated, without deciding in any way upon Dr. Steele's offer.

Whenever an election took place, they required a Board of Education to instruct them how to vote. There was room for a sweeping reform in the Local Government Board, in the collection of taxes and in the election of gentlemen to administer the laws of the country. The whole system might be simplified considerably and the cost reduced enormously. They knew that if a local board wished to borrow any money, it cost them a great deal to obtain tke powers enabling them to do so. They had to go to London, and sometimes their application was postponed from year to year. He maintained that if a local authority wanted to make any alteration or extension, and could get people to advance them the money, they had a right to do so without wasting BO much time and money as was done at the present time. (Hear, hear.) We were overdone in this country by centralisation, and he believed more so in Ireland than in England. Very few of the men who held high positions and earned large salaries in Ireland were gentlemen of the sister isle. Mr. Herbert Gladstone had said it was the worst governed country in Europe. That was a very strong assertion to make, but it was a well-known fact that although it was the poorest country in the world, it was most expensively governed. The Lend-Lieutenant received £20,000 a year, whereas the President of the United States only got £lO,OOO. He thought they might hope that as long as Mr. Gladstone was spared, and had health and strength, that there was a great future in store for the sister isle across the Channel. He be-

lieved he was prepared, if he was only backed by the Liberals of this country, to extend to Ire- land some measure of local self-government. All these reforms he (the Chairman) had mentioned might be explained hi a series of lectures such as they had had in Woolton during the past winter by the editor of the Financial Reform Almanack. He should like a gentleman of this kind brought into Widnes. (Hear, hear.) He did not wish to have a big meeting in the Drill Hall. He would prefer a smaller meeting in a school-room where they could invite their Conservative friends. If they could only get them to listen to these reasonable propositions, they would agree that the reforms were for the benefit of the country. The Liberals were often told that they would dis- member the empire, but the party who would dismember the empire, or smash up the British constitution, were those who would try to stem the course of progressive legislation. He thanked those present for again appointing him their chairman, and Mr. Wright for the kind manner in which he had referred to his services which were very small indeed. He trusted that next year would be better than the last, and that with the assistance of their very able secretary, they would secure a further triumph. (Applause.) The meeting then terminated.
ST. PETER'S CHURCH TEA PARTY.

The annual tea party in connection with St. Peter's Church took place in the Warrington Public Hall, on Mon- day evening, when about 400 persons partook of tea. A meeting was afterwards held, presided over by Mr. Peter Stubs.

The CILLIRMAN, in addressing the meeting, said he was very glad to find himself in the midst of so large a gather- ing of persons who had come to support the work of the parish of St. Peter's, and he was only sorry that Sir Gilbert Greenell, who was away from home, could not be present to take the chair. As to what had been done, there could be no doubt in the mind of any of them that it had been done for the good of the district, but Mr. Schonberg would tell them about this, and as there was a long programme to go through, he would not occupy the time of the meeting by making a speech. The Rev. M. SCHONBERG then addressed the meeting. He adverted to the meeting held at that hall on the previous Monday, and said that the chairman in his able speech advocated education and he agreed with him in every respect, . but there was something that made him feel very touchy about education. What was educa- tion? Learning geography, aritmetic, tlec., was all very good, but there was something higher, and he would advo- cate the highest order of education, and so advocate the people that they would be fitted for the world to come. He did not intend to criticise the remarks of the chairman at the previous meeting, for as he said at the commencement he agreed with evetything he had said, but that chairman was wanting a school, and there was little doubt that with a little energy he would get it. For the last twelve years, he (Mr. SchOnberg) had been harping upon one string, and he had had one object in view, and that was St. Peter's Church. They started a subscription last year, and they had collected £2lO, and £lOO more was promised. This ex- seeded his utmost expectation, and he was heartily thank- ful for what had been received. Lord Winmarleigh and Sir Gilbert Greenall had promised £2OO each, but these were offered conditionally. Lord Winmirleigh had very judiciously said that he offered £2OO if all the money was milected in the year 1883. What he (the speaker) asked for, was not a grand church and a grand organ, but a plain building, and he thought with a little application they would obtain one. His people had wanted a church for a long time, and letters had been sent to the newspapers charging him with not building one, but a church like every other building must be built with money. He was looking forward hopefully to the time when they would have a church, and if he was not allowed to finish it let him in the name of God begin it. (Applause.) The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON expressed his sympathy with Mr. Schonberg in his work. He thought that Trinity was so well represented that evening that there was no necessity for him to express his feelings on that occasion. He thought it was well for them to come together on those occasions and lend each other a helping hand, and thus show people that they were united, and that small matters were not enough to damp their ardour and paralyse their work. It was an important matter that they should be united and work harmoniously together. The time had gone by, he thought, for talking about high church and low church, and the great point in the future would be church or no church. He thought that a man who quarrelled about trifles was not wise, but when it was applied to the church it was sinful. (Applause.) The programme was a varied one, and was gone through creditably, several of the pieces being encored. It con- sisted of the following :—Song, "The old sexton," Mr. A. J. Thornley ; song, "Killarney," Miss Woods; song, "Mary of Argyle," Mr. Reddish:; recitation, "Christmas Day in a Workhouse," Mr. C. Furness; song, " Sailing,' • Mr. Booth; song, "Tit for tat," Miss Essenhigh ; comic song, "Policeman X 89," Mr. G. "Very suspicious," Messrs. Parkinson and Westbrook song, "The lost chord," Miss Essenhigh ; sons, "Old England for ever," Mr. Booth. Mr. Lloyd, of Salford presided at the piano. Mr. SCRoNBERG, JUN., moved a vote of thanks to the tea makers and to all those who had contributed towards the evenings entertainment. Mr. SCHONDERG, SEN.; seconded the motion, au I it was carried, and the meeting was brought to a close.
THE PROPOSED ACCIDENT HOSPITAL FOR RUNCORN.

On Thursday evening a meeting of the committee formed to consider the advisability of establishing an Accident Hos- pital for Runcorn met in the Town Hall, under the presi- dency of the Rev. Canon Barclay. There were also present the Revs. J. Lockwood, E. Williams, Dr. Steele, Messrs. S. Taylor Guest, T. Handley Dr. Mouritz, J. W. Lightburn, J. Meadowcroft, and W. Brooks.—Mr. T. Handley (late chair- man of the Widnes Accident Hospital) was appointed a member of the committee.—Dr. STEELE said from enquiries be had made, he had discovered that the law allowed an Accident Hospital to be supported out of the rates, as was 'done at Widnes. He, however, did not like the idea of saddling the rates with the expense. He felt some pride in the fact that the rates at Runcorn were lower than most other towns, and helpreferred that the proposed hospital should be supported entirely by voluntary contributions. He had been through the Widnes Hospital with Mr. Carey, and he was highly pleased with everything he saw. The hospital was a model one, and one of the cleanest and brightest places he had ever visited. The original cost was mainly borne by the manufacturers, the balance being paid by money borrowed on the rates. He had been supplied with a copy of the rules in force at Widnes, and he thought they could not do better than adopt them at Runcorn. Patients, while in the hospital, paid at the rate of is. per day, and this removed them from depending upon charity. He thought respectable people did not like to be bounden to a charity. At some of the Widnes works there was a rule that when a man was injured at his employment, he should be supported in the hospital by con- tributions from the Work's Club, and he (Dr. Steele) felt sure similar arrangements could be effected at Runcorn. At the public meeting he stated that there were only about two or three accidents during the year, but Dr. Mouritz, the surgeon, had told him there were about 20 cases during that period, which might require hospital accommodation.—Dr. Motruterz strongly advised the committee to follow on the lines of the Widnes Accident Hospital, which he remarked was the most perfect for a country district that be knew.—lt was stated that the cost of floating the hospital would be about £lOO, and the sum required annually for its maintenance about £lso.—Dr. STEELE proposed, and Mr. TAYLOR seconded, a motion that in case a hospital could be established its maintenance be covered by voluntary con- tributions. An amendment was moved by the Rev. E. WILLIAMS, seconded by Mr. T. HANDLEY, that the hospital be established by voluntary contributions, and afterwards be maintained out of the rates —Only three votes were given for the amendment, and the original motion was carried.— Mr. T. Handley declined to accept the secretaryship, which was offered him, and on the motion of Mr. HANDLEY seconded by Mr. TAYLOR, Mr. Lightburn was appointed to the post. Dr. Mouritz was appointed a member of the com- mittee. It was resolved that circulars stating what had been done should be printed, and subscriptions asked for; and the proceedings terminated.

A SHIP DISABLED AT SEA : EIGHT LIVES Lost —An Ex- change Company's telegram says: The lin:line has arrived at Colombo with her bowsprit sprung and her decks swept. She has also lost her boats and sustained other serious damage. Her captain, first and second officers, and five of the crew were drowned. The weather had been fearful.

div.head: COLLISION ON THE MERSEY BELOW RUNCORN.
div.p: COLLISION ON THE MERSEY BELOW RUNCORN.
A MAN KILLED.

Mr. J. E. Worsley, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Board-room, Cemetery, Runcorn, on Monday, on the body of Edward Kinsella, a seaman, on board the smack Alert, who met his death during a collision between that vessel and the flat Yankee, on Friday at midnight. Mr. Peter Sinnott was foreman of the jury. Mr. Robert Raw- linson, engineer, and Mr. Benjamin Edwards, sailing super- intendent, represented the Bridgewater Navigation Company. Objection was taken to their presence, on the ground that ,the witnesses who were servants of the Company would be afraid to speak fully, but the Coroner said the Company had every right to be represented, and he would protect the in- terests of justice. Mr. Grundy, the Company's manager, Liverpool, also appeared. The Coroner said the Company was already sufficiently represented.—Mr. Grundy: I am the representative.—Mr. Fairhurst: It is the unanimous opinion of the jury that the Company is sufficiently repre- sented.—Eventually Mr. Rawlinson retired, and Mr. Grundy took his place. The nature of the accident by which the deceased was killed is explained by the evidence below.— Martin Byrne, of Wicklow, said he was master of the smack Alert, belonging to Mr. Joseph McCarrall. The body which the jury had viewed was that of Edward Kinsella, seaman, of Ne icklew. He was about 70 years of age. He acted as mate of the Alert. The Alert left Runcorn on Friday, bound for Wicklow with coals. Below Garstou they attempted to cross to New Ferry, and ran aground. He at once lowered the sails and cast anchor. About midnight the vessel floated again, and he gave her plenty of chain to hold her. The vessel did not drag the anchor, and he had about 25 fathoms of chain out. She lay "head on" to the anchor. He saw the steamer Helen coming up the river about half-past twelve. She was a long way off, towing a nueter of flats. The smack was showing a white light at the forestay, where it had been placed at eleven o'clock be- fore she floated. He (witness) stood by the helm and steered the smack to the tide. Up to this time the deceased had been in the cabin, but he now came on deck and went forward. It was a strong flood tide, and the steamer and the fiats appeared to make straight for the smack. The steamer, however, passed on the port bow, clearing the smack by about the length of herself. A person on board the steamer shouted to him (witness) to port his helm, and he replied that he could do no more, as the helm was theft "hard to port against the rail." One of the flits behind the steamer struck the smack with a sliding blow, and the next one " hooked" their bows and the forestay with his anchor, having nrst amen in the bowsprit. This broke the chain, and the smack was dragged round by the flat, to which he made the former fast. The steamer stopped when the collision took place. He heard deceased say twice "I'm killed," and on going to see what was the matter he found him lying alongside the hatch on the starboard side. The vessel was lying out of the navigable channel between Eastham and the Snuff Mills.—Griffith Jones, of 49, Wellington-street, Runcorn, said he was captain of the steamer Helen, which was owned by the Bridgewater Navigation Company, Limited. On Friday night he went up the river with 15 flats. They left Duke's Dock, Liverpool. at ten minutes to twelve. When they were above the Dingle, and whilst he was in the cabin, he heard the mate shout: "Flat ahoy! Sheer off. Why didn't you pull your light up sooner." He (witness) then ran to the bridge, and shouted to the fletrnen to took out. The Helen , was then hard to port. He saw a light on board the smack just about two feet above the rail. The night was very dark, and although he did not see the collision he could tell one had occurred by his ropes. Before he went into the cabin, about five minutes before the collision, he had looked ahead with the glasses, and found that the road was quite clear. Had there been a white light ahead he should have seen it. The position in which the lamp was on the smack was not the right one. It should have been twelve feet above the rail. The mate was in charge of the steamer when they left the dock. The steamer and the flats were in the navigable channel; in the usual track they travelled in in the night time.—ln answer to the foreman, witness said all the crew were sober.—Thotnas Smith, of Belvedere Terrace, Runcorn, mate on board the steamer &len, said the crew consisted of four men, besides the captain, the engineer, and himself. Until they were twice the length of the steamer from the smack, her light did not become visible from the steamer's port bow. The light was only two or three feet higher than the rail. As soon as he saw the light he ordered the helm to be put hard to port. He could not see anyone on board the smack, it was so dark, and he shouted "Flat ahoy! Why hadn't you your light up sooner." If there had been a light he should have seen it. The light ought to have been net less than twelve feet above the rail. He (witness) looked through the glasses after the captain went below. He could see nothing. When he saw the light the collision was inevitable. Alfred Gough, of Bridgewater- street, seaman on the Helen, said at midnight on Friday he was keeping the look out. Just above Knott's Hole he saw saw a flat about twice the length of the steamer ahead, a little off the port side. He then saw a light very suddenly, and he called to the mate, who gave orders to put the laetm hard to port. The mate shouted to the flat to " Sheer in," and asked those on board why the light was not shown sooner. The light was on the stay about two feet'above the rail.—Thomas Hughes, of Bridgewater-street, Runcorn, sea- man on board the Helen, deposed that at the time in ques- tion he was steering the steamer. Until the steamer was two lengths off the Alert he did not see the latter, and he immediately received orders from the mate to port the helm, which he did. Immediately afterwards the collision occurred. He corroborated the evidence of the other witnesses as to the light.—Thomas Bate, of Barnton, near Northwlch, master of the flat Yankee, stated that the Yankee collided with the Alert. He was close upon the Alert before he saw the light, which was not very high. A light could be seen on that night at a distance of 100 yards.—The Deputy Coroner said he did not intend to take up their time in going through the evidence, because many of the jury were so conversant with marine affairs, and had taken such an intelligent Interest in what had occurred, that they would be able to form an opinion without his summarising the evidence. The whole matter was a question entirely of negligence— whether they thought the captain of the steamer negligently conducted his steamer, or whether the accident occurred threugh the light on the smack not being properly eadeibited. If they came to the conclusion that there had bee* negligeece, the verdict must be the very serious one of manslaughter, but if they formed an opposite opinion the verdict would be one of accidental death.—The jury, after a consultation of about 20 minutes duration, recorded a verdict of "Accidental death."
Messrs. Ziba Armitage and James 3larson took their seats on the bench for the first time as county magis- trates on Wednesday, at the Warrington County Petty Sessions.

MANCHESTER AND LIVERPOOL DISTRICT BANE.—Owing to the death of Mr. Thomas Cooke, late chairman and managing director of this bank, certain changes in the management have been made. We understand that Mr. Jas. Halliday retains his present position of managing director, and that Mr. William Tipping the manager at the Head Office has been appointed a managing director of the bank, which position he will occupy in conjunction with Mr. Halliday. The other arrangements at the Head Office are that Mr. William Cochrane, the present sub-manager, has been appointed manager; Mr. Andrew Bennie, the present cashier, has been appointed sub-manager; and 11.1r.Frank Wool- ley Hyde has been appointed cushier, and is authorised to sign for the manager. The authority to Mr. Robert Meikle to sign for the manager in correspondence has been extended to include drafts and official documents.
